[§](https://docs.rs#other-projects-simplifying-java-and-rust-communication)Other Projects Simplifying Java and Rust Communication

- Consider [JNR](https://github.com/jnr/jnr-ffi/)if you just need to use a native library with C interface
- Watch OpenJDK [Project Panama](https://jdk.java.net/panama/)which aims to enable using native libraries with no JNI code
- Consider [GraalVM](http://www.graalvm.org/docs/why-graal/#for-java-programs)— a recently released VM that gives zero-cost interoperability between various languages (including Java and[Rust](http://www.graalvm.org/docs/reference-manual/languages/llvm/#running-rust)compiled into LLVM-bitcode)
- See a [plugin](https://github.com/questdb/rust-maven-plugin/)for invoking cargo from Java Maven builds

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [jni_sys](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/index.html)as sys;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [descriptors](https://docs.rs/descriptors/index.html)
- Descriptors for classes and method IDs.
- [elements](https://docs.rs/elements/index.html)
- Helpers for accessing array elements
- [errors](https://docs.rs/errors/index.html)
- Error types and utilities.
- [exceptions](https://docs.rs/exceptions/index.html)
- Reference type implementations and API bindings for various `java.lang`Exceptions
- [ids](https://docs.rs/ids/index.html)
- JNI identifiers for methods and fields
- [objects](https://docs.rs/objects/index.html)
- Reference type implementations and API bindings for various `java.lang`Objects
- [refs](https://docs.rs/refs/index.html)
- Base support for reference types and auto-release wrappers like `refs::Auto``refs::Global`
- [signature](https://docs.rs/signature/index.html)
- Parser for java type signatures.
- [strings](https://docs.rs/strings/index.html)
- Handling of strings in Java’s [modified UTF-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8#Modified_UTF-8)encoding, including conversion to and from Rust strings (which use standard UTF-8).
- [vm](https://docs.rs/vm/index.html)
- Java VM interface.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- [bind_](https://docs.rs/macro.bind_java_type.html)- java_ - type
- Binds a Java class to a Rust type with constructors, methods, fields, and native methods.
- [jni_](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_cstr.html)- cstr
- Converts UTF-8 string literals to a MUTF-8 encoded CStr literal.
- [jni_sig](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig.html)
- Parses a JNI method or field signature at compile time.
- [jni_](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig_cstr.html)- sig_ - cstr
- Parses a JNI method or field signature at compile time and returns a CStr literal.
- [jni_](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig_jstr.html)- sig_ - jstr
- Parses a JNI method or field signature at compile time and returns a `&'static JNIStr`.
- [jni_](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig_str.html)- sig_ - str
- Parses a JNI method or field signature at compile time and returns a `&str`literal.
- [jni_str](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_str.html)
- Converts UTF-8 string literals to a MUTF-8 encoded `&'static JNIStr`.
- [native_](https://docs.rs/macro.native_method.html)- method
- Create a compile-time type-checked `NativeMethod`for registering native methods with the JVM.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)
- A non-transparent wrapper around a raw `sys::JNIEnv`
- [EnvOutcome](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvOutcome.html)
- An opaque wrapper around an `Outcome<T, Error>``ErrorPolicy``Env`
- [EnvUnowned](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvUnowned.html)
- Represents an external (unowned) JNI stack frame and thread attachment that was passed to a native method call.
- [JNIVersion](https://docs.rs/struct.JNIVersion.html)
- JNI Version
- [Monitor](https://docs.rs/struct.MonitorGuard.html)- Guard
- Guard for a lock on a java object. This gets returned from the `lock_obj`method.
- [Native](https://docs.rs/struct.NativeMethod.html)- Method
- Native method descriptor for use with `Env::register_native_methods`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValue.html)
- A Java borrowed local reference or primitive value.
- [JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValueOwned.html)- Owned
- A Java owned local reference or primitive value.
- [Outcome](https://docs.rs/enum.Outcome.html)
- The outcome of an operation that may succeed, fail with an error, or panic.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [JNIEnv](https://docs.rs/type.JNIEnv.html)- Deprecated
- An FFI safe alias for `EnvUnowned`for (safer) compatibility with existing code.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [jni_](https://docs.rs/attr.jni_mangle.html)- mangle
- Export a Rust function with a JNI-compatible, mangled method name.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/jni/0.22.4/src/jni/lib.rs.html

# jni/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![allow(clippy::upper_case_acronyms)]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)// TODO: https://github.com/jni-rs/jni-rs/issues/348
[4](https://docs.rs#4)#![allow(clippy::not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref)]
[5](https://docs.rs#5)#![deny(missing_debug_implementations)]
[6](https://docs.rs#6)
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! # Safe JNI Bindings in Rust
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! This crate provides a (mostly) safe way to interface with Java and Kotlin
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! using the Java Native Interface (JNI).
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! ## Getting Started by implementing a native method
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Lets write some Java code that defines a native method and then implement it
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! in Rust.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ### The Java side
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! First, you need a Java class definition. `HelloWorld.java`:
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```java
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! class HelloWorld {
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!     // This declares that the static `hello` method will be provided
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!     // by a native library.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!     private static native String hello(String input);
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!     static {
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!         // This actually loads the shared object that we'll be creating.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!         // The actual location of the .so or .dll may differ based on your
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         // platform.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!         System.loadLibrary("mylib");
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!     }
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!     // The rest is just regular ol' Java!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!     public static void main(String[] args) {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!         String output = HelloWorld.hello("World");
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!         System.out.println(output);
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!     }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! }
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! ```
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! Compile this to a class file with `javac HelloWorld.java`.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! Trying to run it now will give us the error `Exception in thread "main"
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! java.lang.UnsatisfiedLinkError: no mylib in java.library.path` since we
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! haven't written our native code yet.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ### The Rust side
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! There are two approaches to implementing a native method in Rust.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! In either case you first need to implement an `extern "system"` function
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! that accepts the appropriate arguments and has a matching return type.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! And then to make the implementation visible to the JVM you can either:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! 1. Export the function from a shared library with a mangled name that the
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!    JVM can look up.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! 2. You can use the JNI API to explicitly register the implementation with
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!    the JVM at runtime using [`Env::register_native_methods`] (in this case
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!    the function name doesn't need to be mangled or exported from a shared
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!    library)
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! The arguments and return type for a native method implementation are
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! documented in the JNI specification under "Design" -> "Native Method
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! Arguments"
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/jni/design.html#native-method-arguments>
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! which can be summarized as:
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! - The first argument is always an implicit JNI environment pointer that
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!   represents the current thread's attachment to the Java VM
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     - Use [`jni::EnvUnowned`] to capture this
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! - Next, if the native method is static, the second argument is a reference
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!   to the class that owns the method.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     - Use [`jni::objects::JClass`] in this case
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     - Alternatively, use [`jni::sys::jclass`] if you want to work with the
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!       raw JNI type.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! - Else, if the native method is non-static, the second argument is a `this`
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!   object reference
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     - Use [`jni::objects::JObject`] or a more specific reference type like
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!       [`jni::objects::JString`] in this case
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     - Alternatively, use [`jni::sys::jobject`] if you want to work with the
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!       raw JNI type.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! - The rest of the arguments are the Java arguments passed to the method:
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     - Java primitive types are passed as their corresponding JNI types (e.g.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!       [`jni::sys::jint`] for `int`)
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!     - Java object types are passed as their corresponding JNI reference
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!       types (e.g. `jni::objects::JString` for `java.lang.String`)
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     - Alternatively you can use the raw [`jni::sys::jobject`] type for Java
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!       object arguments if you want to work with the raw JNI types.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! - The return type is the Java return type mapped in the same way as the
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!   arguments
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! #### Exporting a native method from a shared library
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! Create your crate with `cargo new mylib`. This will create a directory
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! `mylib` that has everything needed to build a basic crate with `cargo`. We
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! need to make a couple of changes to `Cargo.toml` before we do anything else.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! * Under `[dependencies]`, add `jni = "0.22"`
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! * Add a new `[lib]` section and under it, `crate-type = ["cdylib"]`.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! Now, if you run `cargo build` from inside the crate directory, you should
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! see a `libmylib.so` (if you're on Linux) or a `libmylib.dylib` (if you are
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! on macOS) in the `target/debug` directory.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! The last thing we need to do is implement our native method.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! As an illustration, we'll avoid using any of the helper macros (like
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! [`jni::jni_mangle`] or [`jni::native_method`]) so it's clear how the
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! underlying API works.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! Add this to your crate's `src/lib.rs`:
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! ```rust,no_run
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! // As we are going to implement a native method in Rust, the JVM is going
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! // to pass us a `jni_sys::JNIEnv` pointer that implicitly represents
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! // an attachment of the current thread to the Java VM.
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! //
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! // `EnvUnowned` is an FFI-safe type that lets us capture the pointer and also
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! // associate the caller's JNI stack frame with a lifetime.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! //
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! // IMPORTANT: The first thing a native method must do is to upgrade this into
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! // an `Env`, which has a side effect of ensuring the `jni-rs` crate is initialized
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! // before any other JNI calls are made.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! use jni::EnvUnowned;
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! // This is the JNI environment interface we'll call the majority of our methods on.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! use jni::Env;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! // These objects are what you should use as arguments to your native
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! // function. They carry extra lifetime information to prevent them escaping
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! // this context and getting used after being GC'd.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! use jni::objects::{JClass, JString};
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! // This type represents an owned, JNI-compatible string.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! use jni::strings::JNIString;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! // This keeps Rust from "mangling" the name and making it unique for this crate.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! #[unsafe(no_mangle)]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! pub extern "system" fn Java_HelloWorld_hello<'caller>(
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     // This captures the raw `jni_sys::JNIEnv` pointer and associates it with the
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!     // caller's JNI stack frame lifetime.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     mut unowned_env: EnvUnowned<'caller>,
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!     // This is the class that owns our static method. It's not going to be used,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     // but still must be present to match the expected signature of a static
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!     // native method.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     //
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     // If we were implementing a non-static native method then this would be
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!     // a `this: JObject<'caller>`, serving as a reference to the instance.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     class: JClass<'caller>,
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!     input: JString<'caller>)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     -> JString<'caller>
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!     // Before we can access JNI, jni-rs needs to know that the thread is
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!     // attached to the Java VM.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     //
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     // Within a native method we can assume the JVM attaches the thread
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     // before calling our implementation, and this is represented
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!     // by the EnvUnowned type.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     //
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     // We use `with_env` to upgrade the EnvUnowned to a Env, which gives us
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!     // access to the full JNI API.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     //
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     // IMPORTANT: Don't use `jni-rs` in any other way within a native method
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!     // until you call `unowned_env.with_env` or `AttachGuard::from_unowned`.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     //
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!     // Internally `with_env()` creates a hidden `AttachGuard`` to track the thread
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!     // attachment explicitly and this will also wrap the given closure with
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!     // `catch_unwind` to ensure that your code can't panic and unwind across
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!     // FFI boundaries.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!     let outcome = unowned_env.with_env(|env| -> Result<_, jni::errors::Error> {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!         // First, we have to get the string out of Java. Check out the `strings`
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!         // module for more info on how this works.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!         let input: String = input.to_string();
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!         // Then we have to create a new Java string to return. Again, more info
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!         // in the `strings` module.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!         JString::from_str(env, format!("Hello, {}!", input))
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!     });
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!    // Finally, we have to resolve the `EnvOutcome` into a concrete return value.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!    //
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!    // Our code above may have failed with a JNI error, or some other
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!    // application-specific error, or it may have panicked. None of these things
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!    // can pass over the FFI boundary back into the JVM.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!    //
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!    // Mapping of errors and panics is done according to the selected
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!    // `ErrorPolicy` trait implementation which is able to use JNI for throwing
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!    // Java exceptions if necessary.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!    //
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!    // This design lets you encapsulate your own approach to forwarding errors
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!    // and panics to Java code and then easily reuse it across multiple native
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!    // methods.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!    //
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!    // In this case we use a built-in policy that throws a Java
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!    // `RuntimeException` with a message containing the error/panic details.
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!     outcome.resolve::<jni::errors::ThrowRuntimeExAndDefault>()
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! }
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! ```
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! The `Java_HelloWorld_hello` function name was mangled according to the JNI
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! Specification, under "Design" -> "Resolving Native Method Names"
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/jni/design.html#resolving-native-method-names>
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! To avoid having to manually mangle the function name, the
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! [`jni::jni_mangle`], [`jni::native_method`] and [`jni::bind_java_type`]
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! macros can all handle this for you.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! ### Final steps
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! That's it! Build your crate and try to run your Java class again.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! ... Same error as before you say? Well that's because JVM is looking for
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! `mylib` in all the wrong places. To tell it where to look you can pass this
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! argument to `java`: `-Djava.library.path=/path/to/mylib/target/debug`. Now,
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! you should get the expected output `Hello, World!` from your Java class.
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! For reference you can find this example in the
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! [`mylib-example`][jni-rs-mylib-example] directory of this repository:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! ## Launching JVM from Rust
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! It is possible to launch a JVM from a native process using the [Invocation
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! API], provided by [`JavaVM`].
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! ## See Also
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!

[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! - The [examples directory][jni-rs-examples] in this repository contains a
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!   variety of examples that illustrate the utility macros provided by this
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!   crate.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! - [Example mylib project][jni-rs-mylib-example] (as illustrated above)

[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! - [`bind_java_type`] for generating full Rust bindings for Java types

[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! - Consider [JNR][projects-jnr] if you just need to use a native library with
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!   C interface
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! - Watch OpenJDK [Project Panama][projects-panama] which aims to enable using
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!   native libraries with no JNI code
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! - Consider [GraalVM][projects-graalvm] — a recently released VM that gives
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!   zero-cost interoperability between various languages (including Java and
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!   [Rust][graalvm-rust] compiled into LLVM-bitcode)

[348](https://docs.rs#348)#[deprecated(
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    since = "0.22.0",
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    note = r#"Since 0.22, `JNIEnv` has been split into `Env` and `EnvUnowned`
[351](https://docs.rs#351)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)- `EnvUnowned` is FFI safe and can be accepted as an argument for native methods
[353](https://docs.rs#353)- `Env` is what provides the full JNI environment API and is not FFI safe.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)To remain safe by default, `jni::JNIEnv` is now an alias for `EnvUnowned` (which is FFI safe).
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)Use `EnvUnowned` to capture a raw `jni_sys::JNIEnv` pointer in native methods, like:
[358](https://docs.rs#358)`pub extern "system" fn Java_HelloWorld_hello<'frame>(unowned_env: EnvUnowned<'frame>, ...)`
[359](https://docs.rs#359)Then use `unowned_env.with_env()` to upgrade it to an `Env` reference.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)
[361](https://docs.rs#361)Most of the time you should temporarily acquire a `Env` reference using:
[362](https://docs.rs#362)- `JavaVM::attach_current_thread` (preferred) or `JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope`
[363](https://docs.rs#363)- `JavaVM::with_env` (if certain that the thread is already attached)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)- `UnownedEnv::with_env()` in native methods
[365](https://docs.rs#365)
[366](https://docs.rs#366)When migrating to 0.22, if you have a mixture of FFI/non-FFI usage of JNIEnv then err on the side
[367](https://docs.rs#367)of renaming `JNIEnv` to `EnvUnowned` because that's safe for FFI and for non-FFI usage there will be
[368](https://docs.rs#368)clear compiler errors if trying to access the real `Env` API through the `EnvUnowned` type.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)"#
[370](https://docs.rs#370))]
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// An FFI safe alias for `EnvUnowned` for (safer) compatibility with
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// existing code.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)///
[374](https://docs.rs#374)/// Since 0.22 ([#570](https://github.com/jni-rs/jni-rs/pull/570)) the
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// `JNIEnv` type was renamed to [Env], which is no longer an FFI safe
[376](https://docs.rs#376)/// pointer wrapper.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)///
[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// FFI usage of `JNIEnv`, within native method arguments, should be
[379](https://docs.rs#379)/// migrated to [EnvUnowned], followed by [`EnvUnowned::with_env`].
[380](https://docs.rs#380)///
[381](https://docs.rs#381)/// To help make this clear and sign post how to safely migrate to the [Env]
[382](https://docs.rs#382)/// and [EnvUnowned] types, we export this deprecated alias with a warning.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)pub type JNIEnv<'frame> = EnvUnowned<'frame>;
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)/// Java VM interface.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)pub mod vm;
[387](https://docs.rs#387)
[388](https://docs.rs#388)#[doc(hidden)]

[391](https://docs.rs#391)    note = "Please use `jni::vm::JavaVM` instead of `jni::JavaVM`."
[392](https://docs.rs#392))]

[432](https://docs.rs#432)// Provides a way to validate all our object bindings in a unit test, considering
[433](https://docs.rs#433)// that the `J<Foo>API::get` functions are only exported with `pub(crate)` visibility.
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//
[435](https://docs.rs#435)// If any typos in method names or incorrect method or field signatures will result
[436](https://docs.rs#436)// in a panic here when the binding initialization fails.
[437](https://docs.rs#437)#[doc(hidden)]
[438](https://docs.rs#438)pub fn __test_bindings_init(env: &crate::Env, loader: &crate::refs::LoaderContext) {
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    objects::JByteBufferAPI::get(env, loader)
[440](https://docs.rs#440)        .expect("Failed to initialize JByteBufferAPI bindings");
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    objects::JClassLoaderAPI::get(env, loader)
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        .expect("Failed to initialize JClassLoaderAPI bindings");
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    objects::JClassAPI::get(env, loader).expect("Failed to initialize JClassAPI bindings");
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    objects::JCharSequenceAPI::get(env, loader)
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        .expect("Failed to initialize JCharSequenceAPI bindings");
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    objects::JCollectionAPI::get(env, loader)
[447](https://docs.rs#447)        .expect("Failed to initialize JCollectionAPI bindings");
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    objects::JIteratorAPI::get(env, loader).expect("Failed to initialize JIteratorAPI bindings");
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    objects::JListAPI::get(env, loader).expect("Failed to initialize JListAPI bindings");
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    objects::JMapAPI::get(env, loader).expect("Failed to initialize JMapAPI bindings");
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    objects::JMapEntryAPI::get(env, loader).expect("Failed to initialize JMapEntryAPI bindings");
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    objects::JObjectArrayAPI::<objects::JString>::get(env, loader)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        .expect("Failed to initialize JObjectArrayAPI<JString> bindings");

[455](https://docs.rs#455)    objects::JPrimitiveArrayAPI_jboolean::get(env, loader)

# Env in jni - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jni/0.22.4/jni/struct.Env.html

`pub struct Env<'local> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A non-transparent wrapper around a raw [ sys::JNIEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/type.JNIEnv.html) pointer that provides
safe access to the Java Native Interface (JNI) functions.

Since [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) is not a type that is publicly constructible, you must obtain a
reference, either through a thread attachment, by upgrading an
[ EnvUnowned](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvUnowned.html) within a native method, or via the (unsafe)

[APIs.](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.AttachGuard.html#method.from_unowned)

`AttachGuard::from_unowned`See:

- `JavaVM::attach_current_thread`
- `JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope`
- `JavaVM::with_local_frame`
- `JavaVM::with_top_local_frame`
- `EnvUnowned::with_env`

[Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) is a non-transparent wrapper that is not FFI-safe, so it must not be
used to try and capture a raw [ sys::JNIEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/type.JNIEnv.html) pointer passed to a native
method.

See [ EnvUnowned](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvUnowned.html) for a wrapper that is FFI-safe and can be used to capture
a

`sys::JNIEnv` pointer passed to a native method.[§](https://docs.rs#overview-of-the-api)Overview of the API

All the [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) methods aim to follow the JNI specification naming closely
enough to make it easier to map between the two. This means that method
names, parameter types, and return types will generally be consistent with
the JNI specification.

JNI APIs that can logically be thought of as methods, such as
`GetObjectArrayElement`, can be found as methods on the relevant Rust type,
in this case [ JObjectArray::get_element](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObjectArray.html#method.get_element).

[§](https://docs.rs#exception-handling)Exception handling

Since we’re calling into the JVM with this, many methods also have the
potential to cause an exception to get thrown. If this is the case, an `Err`
result will be returned with the error kind [ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException). Note
that this will

*not*clear the exception - it’s up to the caller to decide whether to do so or to let it continue being thrown.

[§](https://docs.rs#references-and-lifetimes)References and Lifetimes

As in C JNI, interactions with Java objects happen through references, either local or global.

This crate provides various safe wrappers around JNI references, such as
[ JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)

`JClass`[and](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JString.html)

`JString`[which all implement the](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JList.html)

`JList`[trait.](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html)

`Reference`By default these types represent local references, and they will be associated with a lifetime that names the local reference frame they belong to.

So for example `JObject<'local_1>`  and  `JObject<'local_2>` are local
reference that are owned by two different local reference frames and
although they may both be usable from a higher stack frame, it’s not
possible to simply move ownership of a local reference from one local
reference frame to another.

A global reference can be represented by a [ Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html), which will wrap one
of the above primitive reference types like

`Global<JObject<'static>>`. In
this case the `'static` lifetime indicates that the reference is not tied to
a local reference frame and can be used from any thread.So long as there is at least one reference to a Java object, the JVM garbage collector will not reclaim it.

Global references exist until deleted. Deletion occurs when the
`Global` is dropped.

Local references belong to a local reference frame, and exist
until [deleted](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.delete_local_ref) or until the local reference frame is
exited. A new local reference frame is entered when a native
method is called from Java, or when Rust code does so explicitly using
[ Env::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame). That local reference frame is exited when the
native method or

`with_local_frame` returns. When a local reference frame is
exited, all local references created inside it are deleted.Unlike C JNI, this crate creates a separate `Env` for each local reference
frame. The associated Rust lifetime `'local` represents that local reference
frame. Rust’s borrow checker will ensure that local references are not used
after their local reference frame exits (which would cause undefined
behavior).

Unlike global references, local references are not deleted when dropped by
default. This is for performance: it is faster for the JVM to delete all of
the local references in a frame all at once, than to delete each local
reference one at a time. However, this can cause a memory leak if the local
reference frame remains entered for a long time, such as a long-lasting
loop, in which case local references should be deleted explicitly. Local
references can be deleted when dropped if desired; use
[ Env::delete_local_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.delete_local_ref) or wrap with

[to arrange that.](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.IntoAuto.html#method.auto)

`IntoAuto::auto`[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime-names)Lifetime Names

This crate uses the following convention for lifetime names:

-
`'local`is the lifetime of a local reference frame, as described above.
-
`'other_local`,`'other_local_1`, and`'other_local_2`are the lifetimes of some other local reference frame, which may be but doesn’t have to be the same as`'local`. For example,`Env::new_local_ref``'other_local`and creates a new local reference to the same object in`'local`.
-
`'obj_ref`is the lifetime of a borrow of a JNI reference, like`&`or[JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html)`&`. For example,[Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html)`Env::get_list``JList``&'obj_ref JObject`.

[§](https://docs.rs#null-java-references)`null` Java references

`null` Java references are handled by the following rules:

- Methods that require non-null references will return [Error::NullPtr](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.NullPtr)if passed a`null`reference.
- If a JNI function returns `null`to indicate an error (e.g.`Env::new_int_array``Err`/`Error::NullPtr``Error::MethodNotFound`
- Otherwise `null`is considered a valid Java reference and is represented as`JObject::null()`

[§](https://docs.rs#a-mut-env-represents-the-top-jni-stack-frame)A `&mut Env` represents the top JNI stack frame

Each `Env<'local>` represents a single local reference frame in the JVM.

A **mutable** `&mut Env` is special: it always represents the *current top*
local reference frame on the JNI stack.

- You need `&mut Env`when creating new local references, since those can only be created in the top frame.
- A shared `&Env`is fine for operations that don’t produce new local references.

If you only have a shared `&Env` but need to create temporary local
references (that won’t escape the scope), you can materialize a new mutable
handle to the top frame using:

- `Env::with_local_frame`- `Env`for it.
- `Env::with_top_local_frame`- `Env`for the existing top frame without pushing a new one.

If you don’t even have an `Env` (e.g. inside a `Drop` implementation), you
can still get one via:

- `JavaVM::attach_current_thread`
- `JavaVM::with_top_local_frame`

(and you can access a [ JavaVM](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.JavaVM.html) via

[).](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton)

`JavaVM::singleton`These APIs are safe because they constrain the new [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) lifetime to the
scope of the call, so any references created cannot leak.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks)Runtime Top Frame Checks

Rust’s type system ensures that a mutable `Env<'local>` only produces
references tied to its frame.

Normally this crate also guarantees that a `&mut Env` represents the top
frame.

However, because the JVM is global and multiple crates may independently use
jni-rs, some valid usage patterns can be misused to create multiple mutable
`Env`s in the same scope. For example:

```
vm.attach_current_thread(|env1| -> Result<()> {
    vm.attach_current_thread(|env2| -> Result<()> {
        // env1 is still mutable, but no longer the top frame.
        // This will panic at runtime:
        JString::from_str(env1, "not valid here").unwrap();
        Ok(())
    })
})
```
To prevent unsoundness, this crate enforces a **runtime check**:

- Creating a new local reference with a mutable `Env`that is*not*the top frame will cause a panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#rule-of-thumb)Rule of thumb

- Keep only one `Env`in scope at a time.
- Always shadow outer `env`variables when introducing a new one.

As long as you follow this pattern, the type system will ensure that local references are only created from the valid top frame.

[§](https://docs.rs#troubleshooting-cannot-borrow-as-mutable)Troubleshooting `cannot borrow as mutable`

If a function takes two or more parameters, one of them is `Env`, and
another is something returned by a `Env` method (like [ JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html)), then
calls to that function may not compile:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn example_function(
    env: &mut Env,
    obj: &JObject,
) {
    // ...
}
example_function(
    env,
    // ERROR: cannot borrow `*env` as mutable more than once at a time
    &env.new_object(
        jni_str!("com/example/SomeClass"),
        jni_sig!("()V"),
        &[],
    )?,
)
```
This comes from the compiler needing to borrow `env` as mutable for the call
to `new_object`, but also needing to borrow it as mutable for the call to
`example_function`.

In the past we used to recommend here that you could avoid this by
reordering the parameters so that `Env` comes last, but in practice this led
to very inconsistent APIs where some functions had `Env` first and some had
it last, which was confusing.

Now the recommendation is to just make sure that reference type arguments are derived before the call:

```
let obj = env.new_object(
   jni_str!("com/example/SomeClass"),
   jni_sig!("()V"),
   &[],
)?;
example_function(env, &obj)
```
Quite often reference type arguments have already been derived in some outer
scope and don’t involve any JNI method calls so this isn’t too bad in
practice and it keeps the APIs more consistent / predictable, with `Env`
always coming first.

[§](https://docs.rs#checked-and-unchecked-methods)Checked and unchecked methods

Some of the methods come in two versions: checked (e.g. `call_method`) and
unchecked (e.g. `call_method_unchecked`). Under the hood, checked methods
perform some checks to ensure the validity of provided signatures, names and
arguments, and then call the corresponding unchecked method.

Checked methods are more flexible as they allow passing class names and
method/field descriptors as strings and may perform lookups of class objects
and method/field ids for you, also performing all the needed precondition
checks. However, these lookup operations are expensive, so if you need to
call the same method (or access the same field) multiple times, it is
[recommended](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/jni/design.html#accessing-fields-and-methods)
to cache the instance of the class and the method/field id, e.g.

- in loops
- when calling the same Java callback repeatedly.

If you do not cache references to classes and method/field ids, you will
*not* benefit from the unchecked methods.

Calling unchecked methods with invalid arguments and/or invalid class and method descriptors may lead to segmentation fault.

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-asrefjnistr-arguments)Zero-copy `AsRef<JNIStr>` arguments

The JNI specification for many functions requires that string arguments are passed as NUL terminated, Modified UTF-8 encoded byte arrays.

Anything that accepts an `AsRef<JNIStr>` can directly accept a `JNIStr`
literal like `jni_str!("java/lang/String")` which will be encoded as MUTF-8
at compile time.

See [jni_str!](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_str.html) for more details.

For non-literal, dynamic strings then you can use [JNIString::new](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.JNIString.html#method.new) to encode
strings as MUTF-8 at runtime (derefs as [ JNIStr](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.JNIStr.html)).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#417-434)#### pub fn [assert_top](https://docs.rs#method.assert_top)(&self)

#### pub fn [assert_top](https://docs.rs#method.assert_top)(&self)

Runtime check that this [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) represents the top JNI stack frame

Any lower-level API that returns a new local reference must call this method to ensure the reference is tied to the correct JNI stack frame.

All safe APIs that return a new local reference already call this but you
may need to call this in `unsafe` code that uses [ crate::sys](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/index.html) functions
directly.

See the safety documentation for [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.AttachGuard.html) for more details.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#451-453)#### pub fn [owns_attachment](https://docs.rs#method.owns_attachment)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#451-453)

#### pub fn [owns_attachment](https://docs.rs#method.owns_attachment)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns true if this [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) is associated with a scoped attachment that
will also detach the thread when it is dropped.

An owned attachment would come from a call to
[ JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope) but only if the thread was
not already attached.

This can be used to recognise when
[ JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs/vm/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope) really needed to attach the
thread, or if the thread was already attached.

This is mostly useful for diagnostic purposes. For example the `Drop`
implementation for [ Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html) and

[will print a warning if they are dropped on a thread that is not attached, which is recognised with this method.](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Weak.html)

`Weak`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#568-589)#### pub fn [define_class](https://docs.rs#method.define_class)<'any_loader, N, L>(

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#568-589)

#### pub fn [define_class](https://docs.rs#method.define_class)<'any_loader, N, L>(
    &mut self,
    name: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<N>,
    loader: L,
    buf: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)<'local>>

Load a class from a buffer of raw class data.

If `name` is `None` then the name of the loaded class will be inferred, otherwise the given
`name` must match the name encoded within the class file data.

Typically the `loader` should come from [ JClassLoader::get_system_class_loader](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClassLoader.html#method.get_system_class_loader) or the
loader from some other application-specific class.

If `loader` is `null` then the bootstrap class loader will be used, which may not be able to
load dependencies of the defined class.

Alternatively, call [ Self::define_class_jbyte](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.define_class_jbyte) if your data comes from a

[or](https://docs.rs/objects/type.JByteArray.html)

`JByteArray``&[jbyte]`.- Returns `Error::ClassFormatError`
- Returns `Error::ClassCircularityError`
- Returns `Error::JniCall``JniError::NoMemory`
- Returns `Error::SecurityViolation``"java"`package tree.

This API catches exceptions internally and is not expected to return
[ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) (unless called while there is a pending exception).

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-note)Portability Note

The JNI `DefineClass` function may not be supported by all JVM implementations, even though
it is part of the JNI specification.

In particular Android’s ART runtime does not support it, since all classes must be pre-compiled into DEX format.

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-note-1)Portability Note

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#694-750)#### pub fn [find_class](https://docs.rs#method.find_class)<S>(&mut self, name: S) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)<'local>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#694-750)

#### pub fn [find_class](https://docs.rs#method.find_class)<S>(&mut self, name: S) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)<'local>>

Look up a class by its fully-qualified “internal” JNI name, via JNI
`FindClass`.

**Note:** Only use this method if you *strictly* need the JNI
`FindClass` behavior exactly, otherwise, it is strongly recommended to
use [Reference::lookup_class](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#tymethod.lookup_class) (cached), [Env::load_class](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.load_class) or
[LoaderContext::load_class](https://docs.rs/refs/enum.LoaderContext.html#method.load_class).

The `name` must be in the “internal” form, with slashes instead of dots,
like `jni_str!("java/lang/IllegalArgumentException")` or an array
descriptor like `jni_str!("[Ljava/lang/Number;")`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

`let class: JClass<'local> = env.find_class(jni_str!("java/lang/IllegalArgumentException"))?;`- Returns a reference to loaded class on success
- Returns `Error::NoClassDefFound``NoClassDefFoundError`exception occurs, indicating that no definition for a requested class or interface can be found (most common failure)
- Returns `Error::ClassFormatError``ClassFormatError`exception occurs, indicating that the class data does not specify a valid class.
- Returns `Error::ClassCircularityError``ClassCircularityError`exception occurs, indicating that a class or interface would be its own superclass or superinterface.
- Returns `Error::JniCall``JniError::NoMemory``OutOfMemoryError`exception occurs, indicating that the JVM reports running out of memory.
- Returns `Error::NullPtr`

This API catches exceptions internally and is not expected to return
[ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) (unless called while there is a pending
exception).

[§](https://docs.rs#android)Android

On Android in particular it’s notable that `FindClass` will not be able
to find application classes when called from a native thread, outside of
a native method call.

[Env::load_class](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.load_class) can work on Android if a loader has been set up for
the current thread (see: [JThread::set_context_class_loader](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JThread.html#method.set_context_class_loader)) and if you
use the `android-activity` crate this may be done for you.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#815-821)#### pub fn [load_class](https://docs.rs#method.load_class)<S>(&mut self, name: S) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)<'local>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#815-821)

#### pub fn [load_class](https://docs.rs#method.load_class)<S>(&mut self, name: S) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)<'local>>

Look up a class by its fully-qualified name, via `Class.forName(<name>, <initialize>, <loader>)` with a `FindClass` fallback.

This is a convenience wrapper around [LoaderContext::load_class](https://docs.rs/refs/enum.LoaderContext.html#method.load_class) with
[LoaderContext::None](https://docs.rs/refs/enum.LoaderContext.html#variant.None).

`name` should be a binary name like `jni_str!("java.lang.Number")` or an
array descriptor like `jni_str!("[Ljava.lang.Number;")`.

**Note:** that unlike [Env::find_class](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.find_class), the name uses **dots instead of
slashes** and should conform to the format that `Class.getName()`
returns and that `Class.forName()` expects.

For example, lookup the class for
`java.lang.IllegalArgumentException`like this:

`let class: JClass<'local> = env.load_class(jni_str!("java.lang.IllegalArgumentException"))?;`- Returns a reference to loaded class on success
- Returns `Error::NoClassDefFound``NoClassDefFoundError`or`ClassNotFoundException`exception occurs, indicating that no definition for a requested class or interface can be found (most common failure)
- Returns `Error::ClassFormatError``ClassFormatError`exception occurs, indicating that the class data does not specify a valid class.
- Returns `Error::ClassCircularityError``ClassCircularityError`exception occurs, indicating that a class or interface would be its own superclass or superinterface.
- May Return `Error::LinkageError`
- May Return `Error::ExceptionInInitializer`
- Returns `Error::JniCall``JniError::NoMemory``OutOfMemoryError`exception occurs, indicating that the JVM reports running out of memory.
- Returns `Error::NullPtr`

*Note:* In order for this API to be consistent with
[ jni::Env::find_class](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.find_class), this API does

*not*directly return

[errors that may come directly from the loader.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.ClassNotFound)

`Error::ClassNotFound`*Note:* Any [ Error::NoClassDefFound](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.NoClassDefFound),

[or](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.LinkageError)

`Error::LinkageError`[errors include the original](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.ExceptionInInitializer)

`Error::ExceptionInInitializer``cause`
exception if more details are needed.[§](https://docs.rs#android-1)Android

This API will notably check the context class loader of the current thread, which makes it possible to associate a thread with an application class loader.

This may be particularly useful for native applications on Android
because native threads will not normally be able to find application
classes through `FindClass`.

If you use the `android-activity` crate, it may set up the context class
loader for you.

Raise an exception from an existing object. This will continue being thrown in java unless
`exception_clear` is called.

Returns [ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) after throwing the exception.

The ‘?’ operator should typically used to ensure that the new pending exception is reported as an error to calling Rust code, allowing the stack to unwind until something decides to catch the exception (or it propagates back to the JVM).

*Note:* that once there is a pending exception then most JNI calls (that are not exception
safe) will return [ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) until the exception is cleared.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

`env.throw((jni_str!("java/lang/Exception"), jni_str!("something bad happened")))?;`Defaulting to “java/lang/Exception”:

`env.throw(jni_str!("something bad happened"))?;`Create and throw a new exception from a class descriptor and an error message.

The ‘?’ operator should typically used to ensure that the new pending exception is reported as an error to calling Rust code, allowing the stack to unwind until something decides to catch the exception (or it propagates back to the JVM).

*Note:* that once there is a pending exception then most JNI calls (that are not exception
safe) will return [ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) until the exception is cleared.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

`env.throw_new(jni_str!("java/lang/Exception"), jni_str!("something bad happened"))?;`Alternatively, see [Env::throw_new_void](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.throw_new_void) if you want to construct an exception with no
message argument.

Abort the JVM with an error message.

This method is guaranteed not to panic, and only calls `ExceptionClear`
prior to calling [ FatalError](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/jni/functions.html#fatalerror). The

`jni-rs` wrapper function does not
perform any heap allocations (although `FatalError` might perform heap
allocations of its own).In exchange for these strong guarantees, this method requires an error
message to already be suitably encoded, as described in the
documentation for the [ JNIStr](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.JNIStr.html) type.

The simplest way to use this is to convert a string to a [ JNIStr](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.JNIStr.html) via

[like so:](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_str.html)

`jni::jni_str!``env.fatal_error(jni_str!("Game over!"))`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1312-1339)#### pub unsafe fn [new_direct_byte_buffer](https://docs.rs#method.new_direct_byte_buffer)(

Create a new instance of a direct java.nio.ByteBuffer

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let buf = vec![0; 1024 * 1024];
let (addr, len) = { // (use buf.into_raw_parts() on nightly)
    let buf = buf.leak();
    (buf.as_mut_ptr(), buf.len())
};
let direct_buffer = unsafe { env.new_direct_byte_buffer(addr, len) }?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Expects a valid (non-null) pointer and length

Caller must ensure the lifetime of `data` extends to all uses of the returned
`ByteBuffer`. The JVM may maintain references to the `ByteBuffer` beyond the lifetime
of this `Env`.

#### pub fn [get_direct_buffer_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.get_direct_buffer_capacity)(&self, buf: &[JByteBuffer](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JByteBuffer.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

Returns the capacity (length) of the direct java.nio.ByteBuffer.

[§](https://docs.rs#terminology)Terminology

“capacity” here means the length that was passed to [ Self::new_direct_byte_buffer()](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.new_direct_byte_buffer)
which does not reflect the (potentially) larger size of the underlying allocation (unlike the

`Vec`
API).The terminology is simply kept from the original JNI API (`GetDirectBufferCapacity`).

Global references take more time to create or delete than ordinary

`Error::ObjectFreed`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1467-1489)#### pub fn [new_cast_global_ref](https://docs.rs#method.new_cast_global_ref)<'any_local, To>(
    &self,
    obj: impl [Reference](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html)<'any_local>>,

#### pub fn [new_cast_global_ref](https://docs.rs#method.new_cast_global_ref)<'any_local, To>(
    &self,
    obj: impl [Reference](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html)<'any_local>>,
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html)<To::[GlobalKind](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#associatedtype.GlobalKind)>>

Creates a new global reference and casts it to a different type.

This is a convenience method that combines [ Self::cast_global](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.cast_global) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.new_global_ref)

`Self::new_global_ref`It first checks if the object is an instance of the target type, and if so it creates a new global reference with the target type.

`obj` can be a local reference or a global reference.

For upcasting (converting to a more general type), consider using the `AsRef` trait
implementations instead, which don’t require runtime checks.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
let local_obj: JObject = env.new_object(jni_str!("java/lang/String"), jni_sig!("()V"), &[])?;
let global_string = env.new_cast_global_ref::<JString>(local_obj)?;
// global_string is now a `Global<JString>` that persists beyond local frames
// For upcasting, the `AsRef` trait is more efficient:
let as_obj_again: &JObject = global_string.as_ref(); // No runtime check needed
```

[if the target class cannot be found.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.ClassNotFound)

Creates an auto-delete [ Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html) reference wrapper around a raw JNI

`jobject` pointer.This may be useful if a third-party library gives you ownership over a JNI global reference pointer and you want to manage it safely in Rust.

If you don’t own the global reference you must not use this function and can instead
use [ Env::as_cast_raw](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.as_cast_raw) to temporarily wrap the raw pointer without taking ownership.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

- The `raw`pointer must be a valid JNI reference of the appropriate type`T`, or`null`.
- The `raw`pointer must not have any other existing wrappers
- You must logically own the global reference and be able to guarantee that it can not
be deleted elsewhere while the returned `Global`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1535-1565)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1535-1565)

Attempts to cast an owned global reference to a different type.

This performs a runtime type check using `IsInstanceOf` and consumes the input reference.

For upcasting (converting to a more general type), consider using the `AsRef` trait
implementations instead, which don’t require runtime checks.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
let local_obj: JObject = env.new_object(jni_str!("java/lang/String"), jni_sig!("()V"), &[])?;

let global_string = env.cast_global::<JString>(global_obj)?;
// For upcasting, the `AsRef` trait is more efficient:
let as_obj_again: &JObject = global_string.as_ref(); // No runtime check needed
```

    &mut self,
    obj: O,
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<O::[Kind](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#associatedtype.Kind)<'local>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1738-1788)

#### pub fn [new_local_ref](https://docs.rs#method.new_local_ref)<'any_local, O>(
    &mut self,
    obj: O,
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<O::[Kind](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#associatedtype.Kind)<'local>>

Create a new local reference to an object.

Specifically, this calls the JNI function [ NewLocalRef](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/jni/functions.html#newlocalref), which creates a reference in the
current local reference frame, regardless of whether the original reference belongs to the
same local reference frame, a different one, or is a

[global reference](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html). In Rust terms, this method accepts a JNI reference with any valid lifetime and produces a clone of that reference with the lifetime of this

`Env`. The returned reference can outlive the
original.This method is useful when you have a strong global reference and you can’t prevent it from being dropped before you’re finished with it. In that case, you can use this method to create a new local reference that’s guaranteed to remain valid for the duration of the current local reference frame, regardless of what later happens to the original global reference.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetimes)Lifetimes

`'local` is the lifetime of the local reference frame that this `Env` belongs to. This
method creates a new local reference in that frame, with lifetime `'local`.

`'other_local` is the lifetime of the original reference’s frame. It can be any valid
lifetime, even one that `'local` outlives or vice versa.

Think of `'local` as meaning `'new` and `'other_local` as meaning `'original`. (It is
unfortunately not possible to actually give these names to the two lifetimes because
`'local` is a parameter to the `Env` type, not a parameter to this method.)

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

In the following example, the `ExampleError::extract_throwable` method uses
`Env::new_local_ref` to create a new local reference that outlives the original global
reference:

```
/// An error that may be caused by either a Java exception or something going wrong in Rust
/// code.
enum ExampleError {
    /// This variant represents a Java exception.
    ///
    /// The enclosed `Global` points to a Java object of class `java.lang.Throwable`
    /// (or one of its many subclasses).
    Exception(Global<JObject<'static>>),
    /// This variant represents an error in Rust code, not a Java exception.
    Other(SomeOtherErrorType),
}
impl ExampleError {
    /// Consumes this `ExampleError` and produces a `JThrowable`, suitable for throwing
    /// back to Java code.
    ///
    /// If this is an `ExampleError::Exception`, then this extracts the enclosed Java
    /// exception object. Otherwise, a new exception object is created to represent this
    /// error.
    fn extract_throwable<'local>(self, env: &mut Env<'local>) -> jni::errors::Result<JThrowable<'local>> {
        let throwable: JObject = match self {
            ExampleError::Exception(exception) => {
                // The error was caused by a Java exception.
                // Here, `exception` is a `Global` pointing to a Java `Throwable`. It
                // will be dropped at the end of this `match` arm. We'll use
                // `new_local_ref` to create a local reference that will outlive the
                // `Global`.
                env.new_local_ref(&exception)?
            }
            ExampleError::Other(error) => {
                // The error was caused by something that happened in Rust code. Create a
                // new `java.lang.Error` to represent it.
                let error_string = JString::from_str(env, error.to_string())?;
                env.new_object(
                    jni_str!("java/lang/Error"),
                    jni_sig!("(Ljava/lang/String;)V"),
                    &[
                        (&error_string).into(),
                    ],
                )?
            }
        };
        let throwable = env.cast_local::<JThrowable>(throwable)?;
        Ok(throwable)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1818-1838)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#1818-1838)

Creates a new local reference and casts it to a different type.

This is a convenience method that combines [ Self::cast_local](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.cast_local) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.new_local_ref)

`Self::new_local_ref`This performs a runtime type check using `IsInstanceOf` and then creates a new local
reference.

`obj` can be a local reference or a global reference.

For upcasting (converting to a more general type), consider using the `From` trait
implementations instead, which don’t require runtime checks.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
let local_obj: JObject = env.new_object(jni_str!("java/lang/String"), jni_sig!("()V"), &[])?;
let local_string = env.new_cast_local_ref::<JString>(&local_obj)?;
// local_string is now a JString<'local> in the current frame
```

#### pub unsafe fn [as_cast_raw](https://docs.rs#method.as_cast_raw)<'from, To>(
    &self,

Attempts to cast a raw [ jobject](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/type.jobject.html) reference without taking ownership.

This method borrows the input reference and returns a wrapper that derefs to the target type. The original reference remains valid and can continue to be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
// SAFETY: we know that raw_global is a valid java.lang.String reference

```
[§](https://docs.rs#errors-6)Errors

Returns [ Error::WrongObjectType](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.WrongObjectType) if the object is not an instance of
the target type. Returns

[if the target class cannot be found.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.ClassNotFound)

`Error::ClassNotFound`[§](https://docs.rs#safety-5)Safety

The caller must ensure that `from` is a valid reference (local or
global) - which may be `null`.

The caller must ensure the `from` reference will not be deleted while
the `Cast` exists.

Note: even though this API is `unsafe`, it will still do a runtime check
that `from` is a valid instance of `To`, so you are not required to know
this.

Note: this API is agnostic about whether the reference is local or
global because the returned [ Cast](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Cast.html) wrapper doesn’t give ownership over
the reference and so you can’t accidentally attempt to delete it using
the wrong JNI API.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2043-2056)#### pub fn [delete_local_ref](https://docs.rs#method.delete_local_ref)<'other_local, O>(&self, obj: O)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2043-2056)

#### pub fn [delete_local_ref](https://docs.rs#method.delete_local_ref)<'other_local, O>(&self, obj: O)

Deletes a local reference early, before its JNI stack frame unwinds.

Local references exist within a JNI stack frame, which would typically be created by the Java VM before making a native method call, and then unwound when your native method returns.

New JNI stack frames may also be created via [ Self::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame).

Typically you don’t have to worry about deleting local references since they are automatically freed when the JNI stack frame they were created in unwinds.

But, each local reference takes memory and so you need to make sure to not excessively allocate local references.

If you find that you are allocating a large number of local references in a single native method call, (e.g. while looping over a large collection), this API can be used to explicitly delete local references before the JNI stack frame unwinds.

In most cases it is better to use [ Auto](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Auto.html) (see

[method) or](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.IntoAuto.html#method.auto)

`IntoAuto::auto`[instead of directly calling](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame)

`Self::with_local_frame`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.delete_local_ref)

`Self::delete_local_ref`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2138-2164)#### pub fn [with_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2138-2164)

#### pub fn [with_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Run a closure with a mutable [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) associated with a new local reference frame.

`capacity` is the minimum number of local references that can be created in the new frame.
it can be seen as a hint to the JVM to pre-allocate space for that many local references
but if more are created then the JVM will transparently allocate more space as needed.

If a frame can’t be allocated with the requested capacity for local references, returns
`Err` with a pending `OutOfMemoryError`.

Once this method returns, all references allocated in the frame are freed.

If you need to return a reference from the frame to the caller then you should either
use [ Self::with_local_frame_returning_local](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame_returning_local) or else create a

[with](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html)

`Global`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.new_global_ref)

`Self::new_global_ref`[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-1)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See top-level [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one
[Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to avoid exposing code to runtime checks for
the top JNI frame (that can panic).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2183-2231)#### pub fn [with_local_frame_returning_local](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame_returning_local)<F, T, E>(
    &mut self,
    capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    f: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T::[Kind](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#associatedtype.Kind)<'local>, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2183-2231)

#### pub fn [with_local_frame_returning_local](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame_returning_local)<F, T, E>(
    &mut self,
    capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    f: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T::[Kind](https://docs.rs/refs/trait.Reference.html#associatedtype.Kind)<'local>, E>

Run a closure with a mutable [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) associated with a new local reference frame, and return
one local reference to the caller.

`capacity` is the minimum number of local references that can be created in the new frame.
it can be seen as a hint to the JVM to pre-allocate space for that many local references but
if more are created then the JVM will transparently allocate more space as needed.

If a frame can’t be allocated with the requested capacity for local references, returns
`Err` with a pending `OutOfMemoryError`.

Once this method returns, all references allocated in the frame are freed, except the one that the function returns, which remains valid.

Since the low-level JNI interface has support for passing back a single local reference from
a local frame as special-case optimization, this alternative to `with_local_frame` exposes
that capability to return a local reference without needing to create a temporary
[ Global](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Global.html).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2259-2268)#### pub fn [with_top_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_top_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2259-2268)

#### pub fn [with_top_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_top_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Runs a closure with a mutable [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) associated with the top local reference frame.

Unlike [ Self::with_local_frame()](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame), this API does not push a new JNI stack frame and so new
local references created in the closure will be associated with the existing local reference
frame at the top of the stack.

Most of the time this API should probably be avoided (see [ Self::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame)).

Only use if:

- You’re sure your code won’t leak local references into the current stack frame.
- OR, you’re sure that the leaked references are acceptable because you know when the top frame will unwind and release those references.

This will have a slightly lower overhead than [ Self::with_local_frame()](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame) (since it doesn’t
need to push/pop a JNI stack frame), but the trade off is that you may leak local references
into the top stack frame.

Keep in mind that deleting local references individually is likely to have a higher cost than pushing/popping a JNI stack frame, so you should probably only use this API if you’re OK with leaking a small number of local references into the top frame and waiting for it to unwind.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-2)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See top-level [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference
per-scope to avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame (that can panic).

[if an](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.JniError.html#variant.NoMemory)

`JniError::NoMemory``OutOfMemoryError` is thrown by
the JVM.This API catches exceptions internally and is not expected to return
[ Error::JavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JavaException) (unless called while there is a pending exception).

Call a static method in an unsafe manner. This does nothing to check whether the method is valid to call on the class, whether the return type is correct, or whether the number of args is valid for the method.

Under the hood, this simply calls the `CallStatic<Type>MethodA` method
with the provided arguments.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-6)Safety

The provided JMethodID must be valid, and match the types and number of arguments, and return type. If these are incorrect, the JVM may crash. The JMethodID must also match the passed type.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2899-2944)#### pub fn [call_method](https://docs.rs#method.call_method)<'other_local, 'sig, 'sig_args, O, N, S>(
    &mut self,
    obj: O,
    name: N,
    sig: S,
    args: &[[JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValue.html)<'_>],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JValueOwned](https://docs.rs/enum.JValueOwned.html)<'local>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2899-2944)

#### pub fn [call_method](https://docs.rs#method.call_method)<'other_local, 'sig, 'sig_args, O, N, S>(
    &mut self,
    obj: O,
    name: N,
    sig: S,
    args: &[[JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValue.html)<'_>],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JValueOwned](https://docs.rs/enum.JValueOwned.html)<'local>>

Calls an object method safely. This comes with a number of lookups/checks. It

- Looks up the [JClass](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JClass.html)for the given object.
- Looks up the [JMethodID](https://docs.rs/ids/struct.JMethodID.html)for the object’s class/name/signature combination
- Ensures that the number/types of args matches the signature
- Calls `Self::call_method_unchecked`

Note: this may cause a Java exception if the arguments are the wrong type, in addition to if the method itself throws.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-16)Example

```
// Call a method with signature: String concat(String str)
let arg = env.new_string("world")?;
let result = env.call_method(
    obj,
    jni_str!("concat"),
    jni_sig!((str: JString) -> JString),
    &[JValue::Object(&arg)],
)?;
```
Note: a traditional, raw JNI signature like `"(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;"` can also be used with
[ jni_sig!](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig.html) but this demonstrates the more ergonomic syntax that the macro allows. See the

[macro documentation for more details and examples.](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_sig.html)

`jni_sig!`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2956-2999)#### pub fn [call_static_method](https://docs.rs#method.call_static_method)<'other_local, 'sig, 'sig_args, C, N, S>(
    &mut self,
    class: C,
    name: N,
    sig: S,
    args: &[[JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValue.html)<'_>],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JValueOwned](https://docs.rs/enum.JValueOwned.html)<'local>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/env.rs.html#2956-2999)

#### pub fn [call_static_method](https://docs.rs#method.call_static_method)<'other_local, 'sig, 'sig_args, C, N, S>(
    &mut self,
    class: C,
    name: N,
    sig: S,
    args: &[[JValue](https://docs.rs/enum.JValue.html)<'_>],
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[JValueOwned](https://docs.rs/enum.JValueOwned.html)<'local>>

Calls a static method safely. This comes with a number of lookups/checks. It

- Looks up the [JMethodID](https://docs.rs/ids/struct.JMethodID.html)for the class/name/signature combination
- Ensures that the number/types of args matches the signature
- Cannot check an object’s type - but primitive types are matched against each other (including Object)

- Calls `Self::call_static_method_unchecked`

Note: this may cause a Java exception if the arguments are the wrong type, in addition to if the method itself throws.

#### pub fn [get_string_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_string_unchecked)<'any_local, StringRef>(
    &mut self,
    obj: StringRef,

Gets the contents of a Java string, in [modified UTF-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8#Modified_UTF-8) encoding.

The returned [MUTF8Chars](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.MUTF8Chars.html) can be used to access the modified UTF-8 bytes,
or to convert to a Rust string (which uses standard UTF-8 encoding).

This entails calling the JNI function `GetStringUTFChars`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-7)Errors

Returns an error if `obj` is `null`.

Gets the contents of a Java string, in [modified UTF-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8#Modified_UTF-8) encoding.

The returned [MUTF8Chars](https://docs.rs/strings/struct.MUTF8Chars.html) can be used to access the modified UTF-8 bytes,
or to convert to a Rust string (which uses standard UTF-8 encoding).

This entails calling the JNI function `GetStringUTFChars`.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-8)Errors

Returns an error if `obj` is `null`.

Create a new java string object from a rust string.

This requires a re-encoding of rusts UTF-8 strings to JNI’s modified UTF-8 format before
calling the JNI function `NewStringUTF`.

To avoid this intermediate copy + encoding, consider using [ JString::from_jni_str](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JString.html#method.from_jni_str), and
using the

[macro to encode string literals at compile time.](https://docs.rs/macro.jni_str.html)

    &self,

Converts a java byte array to a rust vector of bytes.

Returns [Error::IndexOutOfBounds](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.IndexOutOfBounds) if one of the calculated indexes in the region is not
valid (in case the array length is changed concurrently).

This API catches exceptions internally and is not expected to return `Error::JavaException`
