    pub ArrayUtils => com.example.ArrayUtils,
    methods {
        // 1D primitive array
        static fn sum_array(values: jint[]) -> jint,
        static fn create_array(size: jint, value: jint) -> jint[],
        // 2D primitive array
        static fn transpose(matrix: jint[][]) -> jint[][],
        // 1D reference array
        static fn concat_strings(strings: JString[]) -> JString,
        // 2D reference array
        static fn flatten_strings(matrix: JString[][]) -> JString[],
    },
    fields {
        values: jint[],
        names: JString[],
        matrix: jint[][],
    },
}
    // Create int array
    let int_array = env.new_int_array(5)?;
    let sum = ArrayUtils::sum_array(env, &int_array)?;
    // Create and use string array
    let str1 = JString::from_str(env, "Hello")?;
    let str2 = JString::from_str(env, "World")?;
    let string_array = env.new_object_array(2, "java/lang/String", &JString::null())?;
    string_array.set_element(env, 0, &str1)?;
    string_array.set_element(env, 1, &str2)?;
    let result = ArrayUtils::concat_strings(env, &string_array)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#type-mappings)Type Mappings

Use custom types in signatures via `type_map`:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::Env;
// First, define bindings for custom types
bind_java_type! { pub CustomType => com.example.CustomType, constructors { fn new() } }
bind_java_type! { pub OtherType => com.example.OtherType }
// Then use them in type_map
bind_java_type! {
    pub Container => com.example.Container,
    type_map = {
        CustomType => com.example.CustomType,
        OtherType => com.example.OtherType,
    },
    constructors {
        fn new(),
    },
    methods {
        fn set_custom(value: CustomType),
        fn get_custom() -> CustomType,
        fn process(input: OtherType) -> CustomType,
    },
    fields {
        custom_field: CustomType,
        other_field: OtherType,
    },
}
fn use_custom_types(env: &mut Env) -> jni::errors::Result<()> {
    let container = Container::new(env)?;
    let custom = CustomType::new(env)?;
    container.set_custom(env, &custom)?;
    let retrieved = container.get_custom(env)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#native-methods)Native Methods

Implement Java native methods in Rust:

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
use jni::objects::{JClass, JString};
use jni::sys::jint;
bind_java_type! {
    pub Calculator => com.example.Calculator,
    constructors {
        fn new(),
    },
    native_methods {
        // Instance native method
        extern fn native_add(a: jint, b: jint) -> jint,
        // Static native method
        static extern fn native_multiply(a: jint, b: jint) -> jint,
        // With error handling
        extern fn native_divide(a: jint, b: jint) -> jint,
    },
}
// Implement the generated trait
impl CalculatorNativeInterface for CalculatorAPI {
    type Error = jni::errors::Error;
    fn native_add<'local>(
        _env: &mut Env<'local>,
        _this: Calculator<'local>,
        a: jint,
        b: jint,
    ) -> Result<jint, Self::Error> {
        Ok(a + b)
    }
    fn native_multiply<'local>(
        _env: &mut Env<'local>,
        _class: JClass<'local>,
        a: jint,
        b: jint,
    ) -> Result<jint, Self::Error> {
        Ok(a * b)
    }
    fn native_divide<'local>(
        _env: &mut Env<'local>,
        _this: Calculator<'local>,
        a: jint,
        b: jint,
    ) -> Result<jint, Self::Error> {
        if b == 0 {
            Err(jni::errors::Error::JniCall(jni::errors::JniError::Unknown))
        } else {
            Ok(a / b)
        }
    }
}
    use jni::refs::LoaderContext;
    // Register native methods by getting the API
    let _api = CalculatorAPI::get(env, &LoaderContext::default())?;
    // Now Java code can call the native methods
    let calc = Calculator::new(env)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#raw-native-methods)Raw Native Methods

For performance-critical code, use raw native methods that receive `EnvUnowned` directly:

```
use jni::{Env, EnvUnowned, bind_java_type};
use jni::sys::jint;
bind_java_type! {
    pub FastCalc => com.example.FastCalc,
    native_methods {
        // Raw method - no catch_unwind, no error handling
        raw extern fn fast_add(a: jint, b: jint) -> jint,
    },
}
impl FastCalcNativeInterface for FastCalcAPI {
    type Error = jni::errors::Error;
    fn fast_add<'local>(
        _env: EnvUnowned<'local>,
        _this: FastCalc<'local>,
        a: jint,
        b: jint,
    ) -> jint {
        // Direct return, no Result
        a + b
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#direct-function-implementation)Direct Function Implementation

Bypass the trait and provide a direct function for native methods:

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
use jni::sys::jint;
bind_java_type! {
    pub DirectCalc => com.example.DirectCalc,
    native_methods {
        fn native_square {
            sig = (value: jint) -> jint,
            fn = square_impl,
        },
    },
}
// Direct implementation function
```
[§](https://docs.rs#class-hierarchies-with-is_instance_of)Class Hierarchies with `is_instance_of`

Declare class inheritance relationships for safe casting:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::Env;
use jni::objects::JObject;
bind_java_type! {
    pub BaseClass => com.example.Base,
    constructors { fn new() },
}
bind_java_type! {
    pub DerivedClass => com.example.Derived,
    type_map = {
        BaseClass => com.example.Base,
    },
    constructors { fn new() },
    is_instance_of = {
        // With stem: generates as_base() method
        base: BaseClass,
    },
}
    let derived = DerivedClass::new(env)?;
    // Use generated as_base() method (performs runtime check)
    let as_base = derived.as_base();
    // Automatic conversion via From trait
    let as_object: JObject = derived.into();
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#private-methods)Private Methods

Create private method bindings for internal use:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::Env;
use jni::objects::JString;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    constructors {
        fn new(),
    },
    methods {
        // Private binding with underscore prefix
        priv fn _internal_get_data() -> JString,
    },
}
// Public wrapper in your own impl block
impl<'local> MyType<'local> {
    /// Public API that wraps the private Java method
    pub fn get_data(&self, env: &mut Env<'local>) -> jni::errors::Result<String> {
        let data = self._internal_get_data(env)?;
        data.try_to_string(env)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-field-names-and-accessors)Custom Field Names and Accessors

Override field names and customize getter/setter names:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::objects::JString;
bind_java_type! {
    pub Config => com.example.Config,
    fields {
        // Custom Java field name
        internal_value {
            sig = jint,
            name = "mInternalValue",  // Java field uses Hungarian notation
        },
        // Read-only field (no setter)
        static VERSION {
            sig = jint,
            get = VERSION,
        },
        // Custom getter/setter names
        data {
            sig = JString,
            get = get_data,
            set = update_data,
        },
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#documentation-comments-1)Documentation Comments

Add documentation to generated methods and fields:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::objects::JString;
bind_java_type! {
    pub Counter => com.example.Counter,
    constructors {
        /// Creates a new counter with initial value 0
        fn new(),
        /// Creates a counter with the specified initial value
        fn with_initial(value: jint),
    },
    methods {
        /// Increments the counter by 1
        fn increment(),
        /// Returns the current counter value
        fn get_value() -> jint,
    },
    fields {
        /// The current counter value
        value: jint,
        name {
            sig = JString,
            /// Gets the counter name
            get = name,
            /// Sets the counter name
            set = set_name,
        },
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#null-validation)Null Validation

Use `non_null` to validate that methods and fields never return null, converting null values into errors:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
use jni::Env;
use jni::objects::JString;
use jni::refs::Reference;
bind_java_type! {
    pub UserProfile => com.example.UserProfile,
    constructors {
        fn new(),
    },
    methods {
        // Shorthand syntax - non_null qualifier
        non_null fn get_username() -> JString,
        non_null fn get_email() -> JString,
        // Optional field that can be null
        fn get_nickname() -> JString,
        // Block syntax with explicit non_null property
        fn get_display_name {
            sig = () -> JString,
            non_null = true,
        },
    },
    fields {
        // Shorthand syntax - non_null qualifier for fields
        non_null username: JString,
        non_null email: JString,
        // Optional field that can be null
        nickname: JString,
        // Block syntax
        display_name {
            sig = JString,
            non_null = true,
        },
    },
}
fn validate_non_null(env: &mut Env) -> jni::errors::Result<()> {
    let profile = UserProfile::new(env)?;
    // These will return Error::NullPtr("Null Object") if the Java method returns null
    let username = profile.get_username(env)?;  // non_null method
    assert!(!username.is_null());
    let email_field = profile.username(env)?;   // non_null field getter
    assert!(!email_field.is_null());
    // This can return null without error
    let nickname = profile.get_nickname(env)?;
    if !nickname.is_null() {
        println!("Nickname: {}", nickname.try_to_string(env)?);
    }
    // Setting a non_null field to null will also return an error
    let null_string = JString::null();
    let res = profile.set_username(env, &null_string);
    assert!(res.is_err()); // Error::NullPtr("Null Object")
    Ok(())
}
```
**When to use  non_null:**

- APIs where null is logically an error but may not throw an exception
- Required fields that should always have a value
- Methods that are documented to never return null under normal circumstances

**Note:** `Error::JavaException` always takes precedence - if a Java exception is thrown, that will be returned regardless of the `non_null` setting.

[§](https://docs.rs#complete-example)Complete Example

A comprehensive example combining multiple features:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
use jni::objects::{JClass, JString};
use jni::sys::jint;
use jni::refs::LoaderContext;
// Define related types
bind_java_type! { pub CustomData => com.example.Data }
bind_java_type! {
    pub CompleteExample => com.example.CompleteExample,
    type_map = {
        CustomData => com.example.Data,
    },
    constructors {
        /// Creates a new instance with default values
        fn new(),
        /// Creates an instance with initial data
        fn with_data(data: CustomData),
    },
    methods {
        /// Returns the current value
        fn get_value() -> jint,
        /// Updates the value
        fn set_value(value: jint),
        /// Processes the data
        fn process(data: CustomData) -> JString,
        /// Creates a default instance (static factory)
        static fn create_default() -> com.example.CompleteExample,
    },
    fields {
        /// The internal value
        value: jint,
        /// The associated data
        data: CustomData,
        /// Global instance counter
        static instance_count: jint,
    },
    native_methods {
        /// Adds two numbers (native implementation)
        extern fn native_add(a: jint, b: jint) -> jint,
        /// Static native helper
        static extern fn native_format(value: jint) -> JString,
    },
}
// Implement native methods
impl CompleteExampleNativeInterface for CompleteExampleAPI {
    type Error = jni::errors::Error;
    fn native_add<'local>(
        _env: &mut Env<'local>,
        _this: CompleteExample<'local>,
        a: jint,
        b: jint,
    ) -> Result<jint, Self::Error> {
        Ok(a + b)
    }
    fn native_format<'local>(
        env: &mut Env<'local>,
        _class: JClass<'local>,
        value: jint,
    ) -> Result<JString<'local>, Self::Error> {
        JString::from_str(env, format!("Value: {}", value))
    }
}
// Usage
    // Initialize API (loads class and registers native methods)
    // (doesn't need to be called explicitly if using any other API method)
    let _api = CompleteExampleAPI::get(env, &LoaderContext::default())?;
    // Create instances
    let example = CompleteExample::new(env)?;
    let data = CustomData::new(env)?;
    let example2 = CompleteExample::with_data(env, &data)?;
    // Use methods
    example.set_value(env, 42)?;
    let value = example.get_value(env)?;
    let result = example.process(env, &data)?;
    // Use fields
    example.set_data(env, &data)?;
    let retrieved_data = example.data(env)?;
    // Static methods and fields
    let default = CompleteExample::create_default(env)?;
    let count = CompleteExample::instance_count(env)?;
    // Cast to base type
    let as_object = example.as_object(env)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-topics)Advanced Topics

This section covers more advanced features and use cases for the `bind_java_type!` macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#native-method-registration-vs-exporting)Native Method Registration vs Exporting

The JVM can discover native method implementations in two ways:

-
**Exporting with mangled names**: The native method is exported as a symbol with a JNI-mangled name (e.g.,`Java_com_example_MyType_myMethod__I`). The JVM automatically resolves these symbols within a shared library.
-
**Registration via**: The native method implementations are explicitly registered at runtime by calling`Env::register_native_methods``Env::register_native_methods()`, which maps Java method signatures to function pointers.

The `bind_java_type!` macro supports both approaches:

[§](https://docs.rs#automatic-registration)Automatic Registration

The generated `{Type}API::get()` method automatically calls `Env::register_native_methods()`
to register all declared native methods with the JVM. This happens when you first obtain
the API reference for the type.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
use jni::refs::LoaderContext;
    // Loads class and registers all native methods
    let api = ExampleTypeAPI::get(env, &LoaderContext::default())?;
    Ok(())
}
```
**Note:** Native method registration happens early, potentially before Java static
initializers run. This means native methods are available immediately for use in static
blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits-of-exporting)Benefits of Exporting

Exporting native methods (via `extern` qualifier or `export = true`) generates JNI export
symbols that the JVM can resolve when loading a shared library:

**Advantages:**

- Native methods can be resolved before you call `Env::register_native_methods()`
- Useful when Java code calls native methods during early initialization
- Standard JNI discovery mechanism

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        // Generates: Java_com_example_MyType_earlyMethod__
        extern fn early_method() -> jint,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#benefits-of-registration)Benefits of Registration

Registration without export symbols is useful in specific scenarios:

**Advantages:**

- Works when your native code is not in a shared library
- Essential for `Env::define_class()`- dynamically loaded classes can still use native methods
- Provides control over when native methods are bound

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods_export = false,  // Disable exports
    native_methods {
        fn registration_only() -> jint,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#combined-approach)Combined Approach

The default behavior exports all methods AND registers them. This provides maximum compatibility:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    // Default: native_methods_export = true
    native_methods {
        extern fn both_exported_and_registered() -> jint,
        // Exports Java_com_example_MyType_bothExportedAndRegistered__
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling-policies)Error Handling Policies

Non-raw native methods that return `Result<T, E>` use error policies to convert errors into JNI
exceptions and default values.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-policies)Built-in Policies

** ThrowRuntimeExAndDefault** (default):

- Throws a `java.lang.RuntimeException`with the error message
- Returns the default value for the return type

** LogErrorAndDefault**:

- Logs the error (without throwing an exception)
- Returns the default value

[§](https://docs.rs#global-policy)Global Policy

Set a default policy for all native methods in a binding:

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods_error_policy = jni::errors::LogErrorAndDefault,
    native_methods {
        extern fn method1() -> jint,  // Uses global policy
        extern fn method2() -> jint,  // Uses global policy
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#per-method-policy)Per-Method Policy

Override the global policy for specific methods:

```
use jni::{Env, bind_java_type};
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods_error_policy = jni::errors::LogErrorAndDefault,  // Global default
    native_methods {
        extern fn quiet_method() -> jint,  // Uses LogErrorAndDefault
        fn loud_method {
            sig = () -> jint,
            error_policy = jni::errors::ThrowRuntimeExAndDefault,  // Override
        },
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-error-policies)Custom Error Policies

You can implement custom error policies by implementing the `ErrorPolicy` trait. See the
[ ErrorPolicy documentation](https://docs.rs/jni/latest/jni/errors/trait.ErrorPolicy.html)
for details on creating custom implementations.

The built-in policies (`ThrowRuntimeExAndDefault`, `LogErrorAndDefault`, and
`LogContextErrorAndDefault`) provide examples of different error handling strategies.

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-methods-and-error-policies)Raw Methods and Error Policies

Raw native methods (`raw`) bypass error handling entirely:

```
use jni::{EnvUnowned, bind_java_type};
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        // No catch_unwind, no error policy for raw methods
        raw extern fn raw_method() -> jint,
    },
}
impl MyTypeNativeInterface for MyTypeAPI {
    type Error = jni::errors::Error;
    fn raw_method<'local>(
        _env: EnvUnowned<'local>,
        _this: MyType<'local>,
    ) -> jint {
        // Direct return, no Result
        42
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panic-safety-with-catch_unwind)Panic Safety with `catch_unwind`

By default, all non-raw native methods are wrapped with `catch_unwind` to prevent Rust panics
from unwinding across the JNI boundary (which will cause the program to abort).

[§](https://docs.rs#default-behavior)Default Behavior

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        // Automatically wrapped with catch_unwind
        extern fn safe_method() -> jint,
    },
}
```
The generated wrapper effectively does:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn wrapper<'local>(mut unowned_env: EnvUnowned<'local>, this: MyType<'local>) -> jint {
    let outcome = unowned_env.with_env(|env| {
        // Your trait implementation called here
        // Panics are caught
        MyTypeAPI::safe_method(env, this)
    });
    outcome.resolve::<ErrorPolicy>()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-catch_unwind)Disabling `catch_unwind`

If you want to allow your native method to abort on panic or you plan to handle panics
yourself, you can disable the `catch_unwind` wrapper:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        fn no_unwind {
            sig = () -> jint,
            catch_unwind = false,  // Disable panic catching
        },
    },
}
```
**Warning:** If your implementation panics with `catch_unwind = false`, it will unwind up to
the JNI boundary and then abort unless you wrap with `catch_unwind` yourself.

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-methods-and-catch_unwind)Raw Methods and `catch_unwind`

Raw methods (`raw`) never use `catch_unwind`:

```
use jni::{EnvUnowned, bind_java_type};
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        // No catch_unwind wrapper
        raw extern fn raw_fast() -> jint,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#type-checking)Type Checking

The macro performs both compile-time and runtime validation to ensure type safety.

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-checks)Compile-Time Checks

When using `unsafe` type mappings (for handles, pointers, etc.), the macro generates
compile-time size and alignment checks:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
#[repr(transparent)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
struct Handle(*const u8);
impl From<Handle> for jlong {
    fn from(h: Handle) -> Self {
        h.0 as jlong
    }
}
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    type_map = {
        // Generates compile-time size/alignment assertions
        unsafe Handle => long,
    },
    native_methods {
        extern fn process_handle(handle: Handle) -> jint,
    },
}
```
The macro validates:

- `size_of::<Handle>() == size_of::<jlong>()`
- `align_of::<Handle>() == align_of::<jlong>()`

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-checks)Runtime Checks

The macro also performs runtime validation during API initialization:

**Reference type validation** (controlled by `abi_check`): For each Reference type in `type_map`,
the macro validates that the Rust type corresponds to the declared Java class using `IsInstanceOf`:

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    type_map = {
        // Validates at runtime that CustomType is actually com.example.CustomClass
        CustomType => com.example.CustomClass,
    },
}
```
**is_instance_of validation** (always enabled): For each type declared in `is_instance_of`, the
macro validates the inheritance relationship using `IsInstanceOf`. These checks cannot currently
be disabled:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    is_instance_of = {
        // Validates at runtime that MyType is an instance of BaseClass
        base: BaseClass,
    },
}
```
**Native method receiver validation** (controlled by `abi_check`): For native methods, the macro
validates that the second parameter matches the method type:

- Instance methods: Must receive an instance object (not `JClass`)
- Static methods: Must receive `JClass`

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    native_methods {
        // Validates receiver is an instance
        extern fn instance_method(value: jint) -> jint,
        // Validates receiver is JClass
        static extern fn static_method(value: jint) -> jint,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disabling-type-checks)Disabling Type Checks

The `abi_check` property controls all validation (compile-time and runtime). In rare cases,
you may need to disable the checks:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    abi_check = UnsafeNever,  // Disable all checks globally
    type_map = {
        unsafe Handle => long,
        CustomType => com.example.CustomClass,  // No runtime validation
    },
}
```
Or per-native-method:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    type_map = {
        unsafe Handle => long,
    },
    native_methods {
        fn no_check {
            sig = (handle: Handle) -> jint,
            abi_check = UnsafeNever,  // Disable checks for this method
        },
    },
}
```
**Warning:** Disabling checks removes important safety validations. Only use `UnsafeNever`
when you’re certain the types are correct and the performance cost of runtime checks is
unacceptable.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-hooks-and-private-data)Custom Hooks and Private Data

For advanced use cases, inject custom data and initialization logic into the API struct:

[§](https://docs.rs#private-data)Private Data

Store custom data in the API struct using `priv_type`:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
struct MyContext {
    counter: std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize,
}
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    priv_type = MyContext,
    hooks = {
        init_priv = |_env, _class, _load_context| {
            Ok(MyContext {
                counter: std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize::new(0),
            })
        },
    },
}
```
The `priv_type` is stored as a `private` field in the API struct and must implement
`Send + Sync`. The `init_priv` hook must be an inline closure that receives:

- `env: &mut Env<'_>`- JNI environment
- `class: &GlobalRef`- The loaded class
- `load_context: &LoaderContext`- Class loading context

The closure must return `Result<PrivType, jni::errors::Error>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#accessing-private-data)Accessing Private Data

The private data is not directly accessible from outside the generated code. It’s primarily useful for internal macro-generated code or when combined with custom hooks.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-class-loading)Custom Class Loading

Override the default class loading behavior with a `load_class` hook:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
bind_java_type! {
    pub MyType => com.example.MyType,
    hooks = {
        load_class = |env, load_context, initialize| {
            // Custom class loading logic
            println!("Loading class: com.example.MyType");
            // Use the default loader for this type
            load_context.load_class_for_type::<MyType>(env, initialize)
            // Or implement custom loading:
            // let class = env.find_class("com/example/MyType")?;
            // if initialize {
            //     env.ensure_local_capacity(1)?;
            //     env.call_method(&class, "someInitMethod", "()V", &[])?;
            // }
            // env.new_global_ref(&class)
        },
    },
}
```
The `load_class` hook must be an inline closure that receives:

- `env: &mut Env<'local>`- JNI environment
- `load_context: &LoaderContext`- Class loading context with helper methods
- `initialize: bool`- Whether to initialize the class

The closure must return `Result<JClass<'local>, jni::errors::Error>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapper-macros)Wrapper Macros

Create custom wrapper macros to encapsulate common configuration across multiple bindings:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use jni::bind_java_type;
// Define common types
bind_java_type! { pub UserId => com.example.types.UserId }
bind_java_type! { pub Timestamp => com.example.types.Timestamp }
// Create a wrapper macro
macro_rules! my_bind {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => {
        bind_java_type! {
            // Inject common configuration
            type_map = {
                UserId => com.example.types.UserId,
                Timestamp => com.example.types.Timestamp,
            },
            native_methods_error_policy = jni::errors::LogErrorAndDefault,
            // Forward the rest
            $($tokens)*
        }
    };
}
// Use the wrapper - no need to repeat type_map or error_policy
my_bind! {
    pub User => com.example.User,
    fields {
        id: UserId,
        created: Timestamp,
    },
}
my_bind! {
    pub Post => com.example.Post,
    fields {
        author_id: UserId,
        posted: Timestamp,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#overriding-jni-crate-path)Overriding JNI Crate Path

If you’ve renamed the `jni` dependency, use a wrapper to inject the path:

```
macro_rules! my_bind {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => {
        jni::bind_java_type! {
            jni = ::my_renamed_jni,
            $($tokens)*
        }
    };
}
```

---

# JavaVM in jni::vm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jni/0.22.4/jni/vm/struct.JavaVM.html

`pub struct JavaVM(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

The Java VM API, including (optional) [Invocation API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/12/docs/specs/jni/invocation.html) support.

An existing JavaVM can be obtained either via [ JavaVM::singleton](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton), or

[in an already attached thread, or a new VM can be](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.get_java_vm)

`Env::get_java_vm`[launched](https://docs.rs#launching-jvm-from-rust)via

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.new)

`JavaVM::new`[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-jni-version-is-14)Minimum supported JNI version is 1.4

The implementation of this crate assumes your Java VM supports at least JNI >= 1.4

The implementation wouldn’t be able to call `ExceptionCheck` without JNI 1.2 and requiring >=
1.4 means we don’t need any runtime version checks for the direct byte buffer APIs.

Since `GetVersion` requires a [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) and is not one of the JNI APIs that is safe to use with
pending exceptions then the implementation is not always able to explicitly assert the supported
version.

[§](https://docs.rs#attaching-native-threads)Attaching Native Threads

Your application always needs to explicitly attach `jni-rs` to the current thread before it can
access the [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) API (most of the interesting APIs are under

[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)

`Env`If you’re implementing a native/foreign method then JNI will pass a thread attachment (in the
form of a raw [ sys::JNIEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/type.JNIEnv.html) pointer that should be captured using the

[type) and converted into a](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvUnowned.html)

`env::EnvUnowned`[reference via](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)

`Env`[)](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvUnowned.html#method.with_env)

`env::EnvUnowned::with_env`Note: [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) is not a

`#[transparent]` wrapper over a [pointer.](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/type.JNIEnv.html)

`sys::JNIEnv`The attachment of the current thread is always represented via an [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) which blocks
the thread from being detached and acts as a marker for a JNI stack frame.

[ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) is only ever exposed in the public API by-reference, and will always borrow from an

[such that it’s lifetime is tied to a fixed JNI stack frame.](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)

`AttachGuard`Unless you are using `unsafe` APIs though, the [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) itself will usually be hidden,
and you will get a

[reference (that borrows from a hidden](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)

`Env`[).](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)

`AttachGuard`This library supports these modes of attachment:

- A permanent attachment with `JavaVM::attach_current_thread`
- A scoped attachment with `JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope``AttachGuard`
- Implicit (“unowned”) attachments, for use in native methods. The thread will never get
explicitly detached by `jni-rs`if we have implicit attachment.

[§](https://docs.rs#local-reference-management)Local Reference Management

Remember that the native thread attached to the VM must manage local references carefully, i.e., do not allocate an excessive number of references and release them promptly when they are no longer needed to enable the GC to collect them.

A common approach is to push appropriately-sized local frames for larger
code fragments (see [ Env::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html#method.with_local_frame) or

[) and](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_local_frame)

`JavaVM::with_local_frame`[for temporary references in loops.](https://docs.rs/refs/struct.Auto.html)

`objects::Auto`See also the [JNI specification](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/12/docs/specs/jni/design.html#referencing-java-objects) for details on referencing Java objects.

[§](https://docs.rs#launching-jvm-from-rust)Launching JVM from Rust

To [launch](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.new) a JVM from a native process, enable the `invocation` feature in the
Cargo.toml:

`jni = { version = "0.22.1", features = ["invocation"] }`The application will be able to use [ JavaVM::new](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.new) which will dynamically load a

`jvm` library
(which is distributed with the JVM) at runtime:[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Build the VM properties
let jvm_args = InitArgsBuilder::new()
          // Pass the JNI API version (default is 8)
          .version(JNIVersion::V1_8)
          // You can additionally pass any JVM options (standard, like a system property,
          // or VM-specific).
          // Here we enable some extra JNI checks useful during development
          .option("-Xcheck:jni")
          .build()
          .unwrap();
// Create a new VM
let jvm = JavaVM::new(jvm_args)?;
// Attach the current thread to call to the JavaVM
jvm.attach_current_thread(|env| -> errors::Result<()> {
    // Call Java Math#abs(-10)
    let x = JValue::from(-10);
    let val: jint = env.call_static_method(jni_str!("java/lang/Math"), jni_str!("abs"), jni_sig!("(I)I"), &[x])?
        .i()?;
    assert_eq!(val, 10);
    Ok(())
});
```
At runtime, the JVM installation path is determined via the [java-locator](https://crates.io/crates/java-locator) crate:

- By the `JAVA_HOME`environment variable, if it is set.
- Otherwise — from `java`output.

It is recommended to set `JAVA_HOME`

For the operating system to correctly load the `jvm` library it may also be necessary to update
the path that the OS uses to find dependencies of the `jvm` library.

- On **Windows**, append the path to`$JAVA_HOME/bin`to the`PATH`environment variable.
- On **MacOS**, append the path to`libjvm.dylib`to`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`environment variable.
- On **Linux**, append the path to`libjvm.so`to`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`environment variable.

The exact relative path to `jvm` library is version-specific.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#207-227)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(args: [InitArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.InitArgs.html)<'_>) -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#207-227)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(args: [InitArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.InitArgs.html)<'_>) -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<Self>

Launch a new JavaVM using the provided init args.

Unlike original JNI API, the main thread (the thread from which this method is called) will
not be attached to JVM. You must explicitly use `attach_current_thread…` methods (refer
to [Attaching Native Threads section](https://docs.rs#attaching-native-threads)).

*This API requires the “invocation” feature to be enabled,
see  “Launching JVM from Rust”.*

This will attempt to locate a JVM using
[java-locator], if the JVM has not already been loaded. Use the
[ with_libjvm](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_libjvm) method to give an explicit location for the JVM shared
library (

`jvm.dll`, `libjvm.so`, or `libjvm.dylib`, depending on the platform).Get a [ JavaVM](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html) for the global Java VM

If no [ JavaVM](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html) has been initialized, this will return

[.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.UninitializedJavaVM)

`Error::UninitializedJavaVM`If a [ JavaVM](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html) has previously been created, either via

[or](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.new)

`JavaVM::new()`[then that](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.from_raw)

`JavaVM::from_raw`[will be accessible as a global singleton.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html)

`JavaVM`This is possible because JNI does not support fully destroying a Java VM and then initializing a new one and so as soon as we have seen a Java VM pointer once, we know it’s the only VM that will ever exist and it will always be valid in safe code.

If your code observes a [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference or an

[(from this crate version) then you can assume that](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)

`AttachGuard`[has been initialized.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton)

`JavaVM::singleton()`Beware that the observation of reference types (such as [ crate::objects::JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html)) only
imply that

[has been initialized if the references are non-null.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton)

`JavaVM::singleton()`One other caveat is that native methods may capture reference type arguments, such as
[ JObject](https://docs.rs/objects/struct.JObject.html), where their lifetime is

*not*tied to a real

`Env`. (And so at the start of
a native method, [may not be initialized even though we can observe reference types).](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton)

`JavaVM::singleton()`In practice though, you can usually assume [ JavaVM::singleton()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.singleton) has been initialized
if you observe non-null reference types, based on the assumption that:

- Before any other `jni-rs`API is used, a native method is expected to use`env::EnvUnowned::with_env``Env`reference, which will initialize`JavaVM::singleton()`
- For any native method implementation to be safe, it must use `catch_unwind`(e.g. via`env::EnvUnowned::with_env``JavaVM::singleton()`“safe”).

Note: that other versions of `jni-rs` within the same application aren’t able to share this
singleton state. So you should not make assumptions about this being initialized as a side
effect of other dependencies using `jni-rs` (unless you are using a re-exported version of
`jni-rs` from that dependency). For example the `android-activity` crate will initialize a
[JavaVM](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html) before `android_main()` is called, but unless you are using the same version of
`jni-rs` as `android-activity` you can’t immediately assume there is a [JavaVM](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html) singleton.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#398-413)#### pub fn [with_libjvm](https://docs.rs#method.with_libjvm)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[OsStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)>>(
    args: [InitArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.InitArgs.html)<'_>,
    libjvm_path: impl [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<P>,
) -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#398-413)

#### pub fn [with_libjvm](https://docs.rs#method.with_libjvm)<P: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[OsStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)>>(
    args: [InitArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.InitArgs.html)<'_>,
    libjvm_path: impl [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<P>,
) -> [StartJvmResult](https://docs.rs/errors/type.StartJvmResult.html)<Self>

Launch a new JavaVM using the provided init args, loading it from the given shared library file if it’s not already loaded.

Unlike original JNI API, the main thread (the thread from which this method is called) will
not be attached to JVM. You must explicitly use `attach_current_thread…` methods (refer
to [Attaching Native Threads section](https://docs.rs#attaching-native-threads)).

*This API requires the “invocation” feature to be enabled,
see  “Launching JVM from Rust”.*

The `libjvm_path` parameter takes a *closure* which returns the path to the JVM shared
library. The closure is only called if the JVM is not already loaded. Any work that needs
to be done to locate the JVM shared library should be done inside that closure.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#488-498)#### pub fn [attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread)<F, T, E>(&self, callback: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#488-498)

#### pub fn [attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread)<F, T, E>(&self, callback: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Attaches the current thread to the Java VM and calls the provided callback with a mutable
[ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference.

If the thread was not already attached then a new attachment is made which will be automatically detached when the current thread terminates.

Calling this in a thread that is already attached is cheap since it will only need to check thread local storage without making a JNI call.

This API requests to permanently attach the current thread but since pre-existing attachments aren’t affected by this API, it should not be assumed that the thread will definitely remain attached until it exits - that is only a request. For example if something higher on the stack has created a scoped attachment then that will take precedence and the thread will not be permanently attached.

You can safely assume that the thread will remain attached for the duration of the callback.

If you’re not sure whether to use [ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) or

[, then you should probably use this API because it increases the chance that future attachment calls will be cheap.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)

`Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope`[§](https://docs.rs#exception-handling)Exception Handling

If the thread is already attached and has a pending exception (before the callback is run), the exception will be stashed and re-thrown after the callback completes to avoid side effects and to also ensure your callback can run un-affected by the pending exception. (this never affects the return value)

If your callback throws an exception this will be caught and returned as an
[ Error::CaughtJavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.CaughtJavaException).

The exception handling policy can be changed via [ AttachConfig::exceptions_policy](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachConfig.html#method.exceptions_policy) and
using

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_with_config)

`JavaVM::attach_current_thread_with_config`[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to
avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame that can panic.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#532-542)#### pub fn [attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)<F, T, E>(
    &self,
    callback: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#532-542)

#### pub fn [attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)<F, T, E>(
    &self,
    callback: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Attaches the current thread to the Java VM and calls the provided callback with a mutable
[ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference.

If the thread was not already attached, the thread will be detached when the callback returns.

Calling this in a thread that is already attached is cheap since it will only need to check thread local storage without making a JNI call.

Attaching a thread is an expensive operation if it was not already attached, so it’s
generally recommended that you should use [ Self::attach_current_thread()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) (requesting to
attach the thread permanently) instead of using a scoped attachment. Using this API may
increase the chance that you incur the cost of repeatedly attaching and detaching the same
thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#exception-handling-1)Exception Handling

If the thread is already attached and has a pending exception (before the callback is run), the exception will be stashed and re-thrown after the callback completes to avoid side effects and to also ensure your callback can run un-affected by the pending exception. (this never affects the return value)

If your callback throws an exception this will be caught and returned as an
[ Error::CaughtJavaException](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.CaughtJavaException).

The exception handling policy can be changed via [ AttachConfig::exceptions_policy](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachConfig.html#method.exceptions_policy) and
using

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_with_config)

`JavaVM::attach_current_thread_with_config`[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-1)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to
avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame that can panic.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#581-650)#### pub fn [attach_current_thread_with_config](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_with_config)<'config, F, C, T, E>(
    &self,
    config: C,
    capacity: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
    callback: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#581-650)

#### pub fn [attach_current_thread_with_config](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_with_config)<'config, F, C, T, E>(
    &self,
    config: C,
    capacity: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>,
    callback: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Attaches the current thread to the Java VM and calls the provided callback with a mutable
[ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference.

This function allows you to customize the attachment process and choose whether to create
a new local frame (with a given `Some(capacity)`) or use the current one (`None`).

Most of the time you should prefer to use [ Self::attach_current_thread()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) or

[instead of this function.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)

`Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope()`The semantics of [ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) are equivalent to:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
     vm.attach_current_thread_with_config(AttachConfig::default, Some(DEFAULT_LOCAL_FRAME_CAPACITY), |env| {
         // Use the Env reference
         Ok(())
     })
```
The semantics of [ Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope) are equivalent to:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
     vm.attach_current_thread_with_config(|| AttachConfig::default().scoped(true), Some(DEFAULT_LOCAL_FRAME_CAPACITY), |env| {
         // Use the Env reference
         Ok(())
     })
```
See [ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)

`Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope`[for more details.](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachConfig.html)

`AttachConfig`[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-2)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to
avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame that can panic.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#713-759)#### pub unsafe fn [attach_current_thread_guard](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_guard)<'config, 'scope, F>(
    &self,
    config: F,
    _scope: &'scope mut [ScopeToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeToken.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)<'scope>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#713-759)

#### pub unsafe fn [attach_current_thread_guard](https://docs.rs#method.attach_current_thread_guard)<'config, 'scope, F>(
    &self,
    config: F,
    _scope: &'scope mut [ScopeToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeToken.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)<'scope>>

Attaches the current thread to the Java VM and returns an [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) for the
attachment.

This is a low-level (unsafe) building block for [ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)

`Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope`[that allows for more fine-grained control over the attachment process and how you borrow an](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_with_config)

`Self::attach_current_thread_with_config``Env` reference from the guard.The given `config` callback is only lazily called if the thread was not already attached and
returns a [ AttachConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachConfig.html) that you can use to customize the attachment.

For example, this can be used to implement your own equivalent to
[ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) like:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
struct Executor {
    vm: JavaVM,
}
impl Executor {
    fn new(vm: JavaVM) -> Self {
        Self { vm }
    }
    pub fn my_attach_current_thread<F, T, E>(&self, callback: F) -> std::result::Result<T, E>
    where
        F: FnOnce(&mut jni::Env) -> std::result::Result<T, E>,
        E: From<jni::errors::Error>,
    {
        let mut scope = jni::ScopeToken::default();
        // Safety: The scope + guard will remain fixed on the stack by keeping the guard
        // private to this function.
        let mut guard = unsafe { self.vm.attach_current_thread_guard(AttachConfig::default, &mut scope)? };
        let ret = guard.borrow_env_mut().with_local_frame(DEFAULT_LOCAL_FRAME_CAPACITY, callback);
        guard.detach_with_catch()?; // return pending exceptions as Error::CaughtJavaException
        ret
    }
}
```
See [ Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread),

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope)

`Self::attach_current_thread_for_scope`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachConfig.html)

`AttachConfig`[for more details.](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)

`AttachGuard`Consider using [ Self::attach_current_thread_with_config](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_with_config) before resorting to this (unsafe)
API.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

The returned guard must be managed according to the general [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) “Safety” rules.

**IMPORTANTLY:** Never give the returned guard a `'static` lifetime by creating a `'static`
[ ScopeToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeToken.html); the guard must be treated as an immovable value on the stack and not be
re-ordered relative to other guards on the stack. See the ‘Safety’ rules for

`AttachGuard`Since the `'local` lifetime for the [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference will come from the `&'scope ScopeToken`
reference, you must ensure that the `scope` is dropped in sync with the guard (to ensure
no local reference types may outlive the attachment).

This can be achieved by hiding the scope and guard from safe code, only exposing a temporary [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)
reference (as in the example above).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#791-805)#### pub fn [detach_current_thread](https://docs.rs#method.detach_current_thread)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#791-805)

#### pub fn [detach_current_thread](https://docs.rs#method.detach_current_thread)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Explicitly detaches the current thread from the JVM, **IFF** it was previously attached
using `JavaVM::attach_current_thread`**AND** if there is no [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) also keeping
the current thread attached (I.e. you have no

[reference in scope).](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html)

`Env`This will always return an error if there are currently any active [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)s
(detaching the thread in this case would effectively turn guards into invalid, dangling
pointers).

Detaching a non-attached thread is a no-op that won’t return an error (assuming there’s no
active [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) as noted above).

This API has no effect on thread attachments that were created outside of this crate’s API (such as other JNI language bindings).

This API is not applicable to scoped attachments because it’s an error to call while there
are active [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)s.

**Windows Note**: On Windows, in the unlikely event that you have multiple fibers scheduled
on the same thread, this API only has an effect within the context of a fiber that previously
attached the thread to the JVM via [ JavaVM::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread).

_**Note**: It’s *rarely* necessary to use this API because a thread that is attached via
[ JavaVM::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) will automatically detach when that thread terminates.

Explicitly detaching the thread could lead to overheads later if the same thread needs to get re-attached.

If there is a need to detach a thread before it terminates, then it’s possible that a scoped
attachment via [ JavaVM::attach_current_thread_for_scope](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread_for_scope) could be used so that the
detachment would happen automatically.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#863-873)#### pub fn [is_thread_attached](https://docs.rs#method.is_thread_attached)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#863-873)

#### pub fn [is_thread_attached](https://docs.rs#method.is_thread_attached)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Returns `true` if the current thread is attached to a Java VM.

Since this calls [ sys::JNIInvokeInterface__1_2::GetEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNIInvokeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.GetEnv), it will also recognize thread
attachments that made without using this crate (such as other JNI language bindings).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#926-936)#### pub unsafe fn [get_env_attachment](https://docs.rs#method.get_env_attachment)<'scope>(
    &self,
    _scope: &'scope mut [ScopeToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeToken.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)<'scope>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#926-936)

#### pub unsafe fn [get_env_attachment](https://docs.rs#method.get_env_attachment)<'scope>(
    &self,
    _scope: &'scope mut [ScopeToken](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeToken.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/errors/type.Result.html)<[AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html)<'scope>>

Returns an [ AttachGuard](https://docs.rs/struct.AttachGuard.html) for top JNI stack frame attached to the current thread.

If the current thread is not attached to the Java VM, this will return [ Error::JniCall](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JniCall)
with

[.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.JniError.html#variant.ThreadDetached)

`JniError::ThreadDetached`This serves a similar purpose to [ sys::JNIInvokeInterface__1_2::GetEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNIInvokeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.GetEnv) in that it
provides access to the current thread’s JNI environment if JNI is attached.

This API can recognize attachments made by other JNI language bindings but will first check
crate-specific thread local storage for an attachment before calling
[ sys::JNIInvokeInterface__1_2::GetEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNIInvokeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.GetEnv).

Consider using [ Self::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_local_frame) or

[as safe alternatives for running code against the currently attached JNI environment.](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_top_local_frame)

`Self::with_top_local_frame`[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

See the ‘Safety’ rules for `AttachGuard`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#971-981)#### pub fn [with_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#971-981)

#### pub fn [with_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Runs a closure within a new JNI stack frame that will be unwound to release all local references created within the given closure.

If the current thread is not attached to the Java VM, this will return [ Error::JniCall](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.Error.html#variant.JniCall)
with

[.](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.JniError.html#variant.ThreadDetached)

`JniError::ThreadDetached`This API can recognize attachments made by other JNI language bindings but will first check
crate-specific thread local storage for an attachment before calling
[ sys::JNIInvokeInterface__1_2::GetEnv](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNIInvokeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.GetEnv).

Internally this calls [ sys::JNINativeInterface__1_2::PushLocalFrame](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNINativeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.PushLocalFrame) with the given

`capacity`, to create a new JNI stack frame, and calls
[after the closure is executed.](https://docs.rs/jni-sys/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jni_sys/struct.JNINativeInterface__1_2.html#structfield.PopLocalFrame)

`sys::JNINativeInterface__1_2::PopLocalFrame`If you’re not sure that the current thread is attached to the Java VM, consider using
[Self::attach_current_thread](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-3)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to
avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame (that can panic).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#1004-1014)#### pub fn [with_top_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_top_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/jni/vm/java_vm.rs.html#1004-1014)

#### pub fn [with_top_local_frame](https://docs.rs#method.with_top_local_frame)<F, T, E>(&self, f: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>

Runs a closure with an [ Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference associated with the top JNI stack frame.

Unlike [ Self::with_local_frame()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_local_frame), this API does not push a new JNI stack frame.

Most of the time this API should probably be avoided (see [ Self::with_local_frame](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_local_frame) or

[instead) unless you’re sure your code won’t leak local references into the current stack frame (or you’re sure that the leaked references are acceptable because you know when the top frame will unwind and release those references).](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.attach_current_thread)

`Self::attach_current_thread`This will have a slightly lower overhead than [ Self::with_local_frame()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.with_local_frame) (since it doesn’t
need to push/pop a JNI stack frame), but the trade off is that you may leak local references
into the top stack frame.

Keep in mind that deleting local references individually is likely to have a higher cost than pushing/popping a JNI stack frame, so you should probably only use this API if you’re OK with leaking a small number of local references into the top frame.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-top-frame-checks-4)Runtime Top Frame Checks

See [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) documentation for rules on limiting yourself to one [Env](https://docs.rs/struct.Env.html) reference per-scope to
avoid exposing code to runtime checks for the top JNI frame (that can panic).

Unloads the JavaVM and frees all it’s associated resources

Firstly if this thread is not already attached to the `JavaVM` then it
will be attached.

This thread will then wait until there are no other non-daemon threads
attached to the `JavaVM` before unloading it (including threads spawned
by Java and those that are attached via JNI)

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

IF YOU ARE USING DAEMON THREADS THIS MAY BE DIFFICULT TO USE SAFELY!

[§](https://docs.rs#daemon-thread-rules)Daemon thread rules

Since the JNI spec makes it clear that [ DestroyJavaVM](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/12/docs/specs/jni/invocation.html#unloading-the-vm) will
not wait for attached daemon threads to exit, this also means that if
you do have any attached daemon threads it is your responsibility to
ensure that they don’t try and use JNI after the

`JavaVM` is destroyed
and you won’t be able to detach them after the `JavaVM` has been
destroyed.This creates a very unsafe hazard if using `jni-rs` due to the various
RAII types that will automatically make JNI calls within their `Drop`
implementation.

For this reason `jni-rs` doesn’t directly support attaching or detaching
‘daemon’ threads and it’s assumed you will manage their safety yourself
if you’re using them.

Note: [ JavaVM::detach_current_thread()](https://docs.rs/struct.JavaVM.html#method.detach_current_thread) is a no-op for daemon threads
because it will only detach threads that were attached via

`jni-rs` APIs.[§](https://docs.rs#dont-call-from-a-java-native-function)Don’t call from a Java native function

There must be no Java methods on the call stack when `JavaVM::destroy()`
is called.

[§](https://docs.rs#drop-all-jni-state-including-auto-release-types-before-calling-javavmdestroy)Drop all JNI state, including auto-release types before calling `JavaVM::destroy()`

There is currently no `'vm` lifetime associated with a `JavaVM` that
would allow the borrow checker to enforce that all `jni` resources
associated with the `JavaVM` have been released.

Since these JNI resources could lead to undefined behaviour through any
use after the `JavaVM` has been destroyed then it is your responsibility
to release these resources.

In particular, there are numerous auto-release types in the `jni` API
that will automatically make JNI calls within their `Drop`
implementation. All such types *must* be dropped before `destroy()` is
called to avoid undefined behaviour.

Here is an non-exhaustive list of auto-release types to consider:

- `AttachGuard`
- `AutoElements`
- `AutoElementsCritical`
- `Auto`
- `Global`
- `Weak`
- `MUTF8Chars`
- `JMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#invalid-javavm-on-return)Invalid `JavaVM` on return

After `destroy()` returns then the `JavaVM` will be in an undefined
state and must be dropped (e.g. via `std::mem::drop()`) to avoid
undefined behaviour.

This method doesn’t take ownership of the `JavaVM` before it is
destroyed because the `JavaVM` may have been shared (E.g. via an `Arc`)
between all the threads that have not yet necessarily exited before this
is called.

So although the `JavaVM` won’t necessarily be solely owned by this
thread when `destroy()` is first called it will conceptually own the
`JavaVM` before `destroy()` returns.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# jni_str in jni - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jni/0.22.4/jni/macro.jni_str.html

`jni_str!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Converts UTF-8 string literals to a MUTF-8 encoded `&'static JNIStr`.

This macro takes one or more literals and encodes them using Java’s Modified UTF-8
(MUTF-8) format, returning a `&'static JNIStr`.

Like the `concat!` macro, multiple literals can be provided and will be converted to
strings and concatenated before encoding.

Supported literal types:

- String literals (`"..."`)
- Character literals (`'c'`)
- Integer literals (`42`,`-10`)
- Float literals (`3.14`,`1.0`)
- Boolean literals (`true`,`false`)
- Byte literals (`b'A'`- formatted as numeric value)
- C-string literals (`c"..."`- must be valid UTF-8)

MUTF-8 is Java’s variant of UTF-8 that:

- Encodes the null character (U+0000) as `0xC0 0x80`instead of`0x00`
- Encodes Unicode characters above U+FFFF using CESU-8 (surrogate pairs)

This is the most type-safe way to create JNI string literals, as it returns a
`JNIStr` which is directly compatible with the jni crate’s API.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

```
jni_str!("string literal");
jni_str!("part1", "part2", "part3");  // Concatenates before encoding
jni_str!("value: ", 42);               // Mix different literal types
jni_str!(jni = jni2, "string literal");  // Override jni crate path (must be first)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use jni::{jni_str, strings::JNIStr};
const CLASS_NAME: &JNIStr = jni_str!("java.lang.String");
// Result: &'static JNIStr for "java.lang.String" (MUTF-8 encoded)
const EMOJI_CLASS: &JNIStr = jni_str!("unicode.Type😀");
// Result: &'static JNIStr with emoji encoded as surrogate pair
const PACKAGE_CLASS: &JNIStr = jni_str!("java.lang.", "String");
// Result: &'static JNIStr for "java.lang.String" (concatenated then MUTF-8 encoded)
const PORT: &JNIStr = jni_str!("localhost:", 8080);
// Result: &'static JNIStr for "localhost:8080" (mixed literal types concatenated)
```

---

# jni_sig in jni - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jni/0.22.4/jni/macro.jni_sig.html

`jni_sig!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Parses a JNI method or field signature at compile time.

This macro parses method and field signatures with syntax like `(arg0: JString, arg1: jint) -> JString` and generates a [MethodSignature](https://docs.rs/jni/latest/jni/signature/struct.MethodSignature.html) or [FieldSignature](https://docs.rs/jni/latest/jni/signature/struct.FieldSignature.html) struct to represent the corresponding
JNI signature. These structs embed the raw signature paired with type information which can be used
for JNI method calls and field accesses without needing to parse the signature at runtime.

This macro can also parse raw JNI signature strings like `"(Ljava/lang/String;I)Z"` in order to
validate them at compile time but it’s recommended to use the structured syntax for better
readability.

**Note:** The signature and `type_map` syntax supported by this macro is also used by the
[ bind_java_type](https://docs.rs/macro.bind_java_type.html) and

[macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.native_method.html)

`native_method`[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

The macro accepts named properties separated by commas:

The parser automatically detects whether it’s a method signature (has parentheses) or a field signature (a single, bare type).

[§](https://docs.rs#properties)Properties

- `jni = <path>`- Optionally override the jni crate path (default: auto-detected via- `proc_macro_crate`, must come first if given)
- `type_map = { RustType => java.lang.ClassName, ... }`- Optional type mappings for Rust types
- `sig = <signature>`- The signature (‘- `sig =`’ prefix is optional for the signature)

The `type_map` property can be provided multiple times and mappings are merged.

The design allows for a `macro_rules` wrapper to inject `jni =` or `type_map =` properties,
without needing to parse anything else.

[§](https://docs.rs#type-syntax)Type Syntax

Note: this syntax for signature types is also used by the [ bind_java_type](https://docs.rs/macro.bind_java_type.html) and

[macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.native_method.html)

`native_method`[§](https://docs.rs#primitive-types)Primitive Types

- Java primitives: `jboolean`,`jbyte`,`jchar`,`jshort`,`jint`,`jlong`,`jfloat`,`jdouble`
- Aliases: `boolean`/`bool`,`byte`/`i8`,`char`,`short`/`i16`,`int`/`i32`,`long`/`i64`,`float`/`f32`,`double`/`f64`
- Void: `void`or`()`or elided return type defaults to`void`

[§](https://docs.rs#java-object-types)Java Object Types

- Fully qualified: `java.lang.String`,`java.util.List`or as string literal:`"java.util.List"`
- With inner classes: `java.lang.Outer::Inner`or as string literal:`"java.lang.Outer$Inner"`
- Default package: `.ClassName`or as string literal:`".ClassName"`

*(Notice that Java object types  always contain at least one  . dot)*

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-reference-types)Rust Reference Types

- Single identifier or path: `JString`,`JObject`,`jni::objects::JString`,`RustType`,`custom::RustType`

[§](https://docs.rs#array-types)Array Types

- Prefix syntax: `[jint]`,`[[java.lang.String]]`,`[RustType]`
- Suffix syntax: `jint[]`,`java.lang.String[][]`,`RustType[]`

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-types)Built-in Types

- Types like `JObject`,`JClass`,`JString`etc from the`jni`crate can be used without a`type_map`
- Built-in types can also be referenced like `jni::objects::JString`
- Java types like `java.lang.Class`are automatically mapped to built-in types like`JClass`

[§](https://docs.rs#core-types)Core Types

- The core types `java.lang.Object`,`java.lang.Class`,`java.lang.String`and`java.lang.Throwable`can not be mapped to custom types.
- Other built-in types, such as `JList`(`java.util.List`) can be overridden by mapping them to a different type via a`type_map`

[§](https://docs.rs#type-mappings-via-type_map-block)Type Mappings via `type_map` Block

A `type_map` block:

- Maps Rust [Reference](https://docs.rs/jni/latest/jni/refs/trait.Reference.html)type names to Java class names for use in method/field signatures.
- Maps Java class names to Rust types (primarily for use with the `bind_java_type``native_method`
- Allows the definition of type aliases for more ergonomic / readable signatures.

Multiple `type_map` blocks will be merged, so that wrapper macros may forward-declare common
type mappings to avoid repetition.

A `type_map` supports three types of mappings:

[§](https://docs.rs#reference-type-mappings)Reference Type Mappings

Map Rust [Reference](https://docs.rs/jni/latest/jni/refs/trait.Reference.html) types to Java classes like `RustType => java.type.Name`:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
type_map = {
    CustomType => com.example.CustomClass,
    AnotherType => "com.example.AnotherClass",
    InnerType => com.example.Outer::Inner,
    AnotherInnerType => "com.example.Outer$AnotherInner",
    my_crate::MyType => com.example.MyType,
}
```
The right-side Java type uses the syntax for Java Object Types described above.

[§](https://docs.rs#unsafe-primitive-type-mappings)Unsafe Primitive Type Mappings

Map Rust types to Java primitive types using the `unsafe` keyword. This is particularly useful
for Rust types that transparently wrap a pointer (e.g., handles) that need to be passed to Java
as a `long`:

These mappings are marked `unsafe` because macros like [ bind_java_type](https://docs.rs/macro.bind_java_type.html) and

[cannot verify type safety between the Rust type and Java primitive type - apart from checking the size and alignment.](https://docs.rs/macro.native_method.html)

`native_method`[§](https://docs.rs#type-aliases)Type Aliases

Creates aliases for existing type mappings using the `typealias` keyword. This can improve
readability in signatures before defining full type bindings:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
type_map = {
    MyType => com.example.MyType,
    typealias MyAlias => MyType,
    typealias MyObjectAlias => JObject,
}
```
Note: Aliases for array types are not supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#method-signature-syntax)Method Signature Syntax

A method can be given in one of these forms:

- `( [args...] ) -> TYPE`
- `( [args...] )`
- `"RAW_JNI_SIG"`

An argument can be given in these forms:

- `name: TYPE`
- `TYPE`

*(with a  TYPE as described in the Type Syntax section above)*

A `TYPE` may have an optional `&` prefix that is ignored

```
const JNI_SIG: MethodSignature =
    jni_sig!((arg1: com.example.Type, arg2: JString, arg3: jint) -> JString);
assert!(JNI_SIG.sig().to_bytes() == b"(Lcom/example/Type;Ljava/lang/String;I)Ljava/lang/String;");
assert!(JNI_SIG.args().len() == 3);
assert!(JNI_SIG.args()[0] == JavaType::Object);
assert!(JNI_SIG.args()[1] == JavaType::Object);
assert!(JNI_SIG.args()[2] == JavaType::Primitive(Primitive::Int));
assert!(JNI_SIG.ret() == JavaType::Object);
```
Traditional JNI signature syntax is also supported:

Explicitly named ‘sig’ property:

With type mappings:

```
const JNI_SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    type_map = {
        CustomType => java.class.Type,
        ReturnType => java.class.ReturnType,
    },
    (arg1: CustomType, arg2: JString, arg3: jint) -> ReturnType,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#field-signature-syntax)Field Signature Syntax

Traditional JNI signature syntax is also supported:

Named:

With type mappings:

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#method-signatures)Method Signatures

Basic primitive types:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!((a: jint, b: jboolean) -> void);
// Result: MethodSignature for "(IZ)V"
```
Java object types:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    (a: jint, b: java.lang.String) -> java.lang.Object
);
// Result: MethodSignature for "(ILjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/Object;"
```
Array types:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    (a: [jint], b: [java.lang.String]) -> [[jint]]
);
// Result: MethodSignature for "([I[Ljava/lang/String;)[[I"
```
With type mappings:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    type_map = {
        MyString as java.lang.String,
        MyObject as java.lang.Object,
        MyThrowable as java.lang.Throwable,
    },
    (a: jint, b: MyString, c: [MyObject]) -> MyThrowable,
);
// Result: MethodSignature for "(ILjava/lang/String;[Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Throwable;"
```
Multiple type_maps:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    jni = ::my_jni,
    type_map = { MyType0 => custom.Type0 },
    type_map = { MyType1 => custom.Type1 },
    sig = (arg0: MyType0, arg1: MyType1) -> JString,
);
```
This makes it possible to write wrapper macros to inject a `type_map` without blocking the use
of `type_map` for additional types.

With named signature property:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: MethodSignature = jni_sig!(
    type_map = { MyType => java.lang.MyType },
    sig = (a: jint) -> void,
);
```
With custom jni crate path:

[§](https://docs.rs#field-signatures)Field Signatures

Primitive field:

Object field:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
const SIG: FieldSignature = jni_sig!(java.lang.String);
// Result: FieldSignature for "Ljava/lang/String;"
```
Array field:

Field with type mapping:
